info.name: Minos Tactical Floor Game API
info.description:
Backend for the Indonesian Navy (TNI AL) Tactical Floor Game.

## Response envelope

Every response, success or failure, is the same envelope. A client therefore has
exactly one shape to unwrap and one place to read an error from.

```json
{ "status_code": 200, "message": "Successfull", "data": { }, "metadata": { } }
```

* `data` is `null` on a 5xx, and on a 4xx when the failure is not attributable to a
  named input.
* `metadata` is present only on paginated list endpoints.

**One response in this document is NOT the envelope:**
`GET /assets/unit-images` returns a binary zip. A client either saves it or
unzips it, and neither can do anything with a `data` wrapper around a zip. Its 304
is likewise bodyless, as a 304 must be.

## Errors

Every 4xx and 5xx body is `ErrorResponse`. Field-level failures carry a map from
the **request field name** to a human-readable reason, keyed exactly as the client
sent it — so `{"errors": {"name": "This field is required."}}` refers to the `name`
field of the request body, not to any internal name.

| Status | Meaning                                                              |
|--------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 400    | The request parsed but a field failed validation — see `data.errors`. |
| 401    | No token, or a token that is expired or invalid.                      |
| 403    | Authenticated, but not permitted. Also: the account is not Active.     |
| 404    | The resource does not exist, or is soft-deleted.                       |
| 409    | A uniqueness constraint was violated (username, email, hull number).   |
| 422    | The body could not be parsed at all.                                  |
| 429    | Rate limited. `Retry-After` says how long to wait.                     |
| 500    | A defect on our side. The body never contains internal detail.         |

## Authentication

`Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on everything except `/auth/login` and
`/auth/refresh`.

Refresh tokens are returned **both** as an `HttpOnly` cookie and, when the request
asks for it, in the response body. Browser clients should rely on the cookie;
mobile and desktop clients have no cookie jar and must use the body. See
`TokenPair.refresh_token`.

request.description:
Exchanges credentials for a token pair.

**Unknown user and wrong password return an identical 401.** Distinguishing
them would turn this endpoint into a username oracle.

403 is returned only *after* the credentials are verified, when the account is
not `Active`. Requiring a valid password to learn that an account exists keeps
enumeration closed while still giving a disabled user a truthful message
instead of "wrong password". The `System` account can never satisfy either
check: its stored hash is not a valid PHC string, so no password verifies.

item.name: Exchange a refresh token for a new access token

request.description:
The refresh token is read from the `HttpOnly` cookie if present, otherwise from
the request body. Native clients use the body; browsers use the cookie.

Refresh tokens are rotated: the response carries a new one and the presented one
is invalidated. A client that replays an old refresh token is rejected, which is
what makes theft detectable.

request.description:
Requires the current password. On success every other refresh token for this
account is invalidated.

The password is passed to Argon2id **byte for byte**. It is never trimmed,
whitespace-collapsed or otherwise normalised — a value that is altered between
being set and being verified means the user can never sign in again, and it is
not reproducible from what they typed.

item.name: Replace which application roles an account holds

variable.description: The account's surrogate id. Never reused.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on **`/system/roles`** — NOT on `/system/users`.

**That separation is the point of this operation.** Every other route under `/users/{id}`
checks `/system/users`, so an Operator who may correct an account's details cannot promote
anybody — themselves included — to Administrator. Bundling the two would mean one grant
bought both, and "may fix a typo in a name" would silently carry "may hand out
Administrators".

**It is also the only thing that distinguishes the two seeded roles.** As of migration
000025, `Administrator` and `Operator` hold the same 32 permissions; this grant is the one
an Operator does not have. A client rendering the role picker should therefore expect a
`403` for anyone but an Administrator — which is a working boundary, not a bug.

The body is the **complete set**, not a delta, so sending the same set twice is a no-op and
a retry is safe. A revoked grant is recorded as a tombstone rather than erased, so
`user_roles` keeps who removed which role and when, and re-granting the same role later
writes a fresh row rather than rewriting history.

An unknown role id is refused **before anything is written**, so a request naming one bad id
leaves the account's existing roles exactly as they were.

response.name: The account with the roles it now holds.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/users`.

**Any** account may be updated; there is no row-level ownership rule. G1 was
answered on 2026-09-14: administration is an out-of-game function, so the Casbin
check on the resource family is the whole rule. See `docs/client-questions.md`.

Casbin still cannot answer "may this Operator update *this* account" — policy
objects deliberately carry no instance ids. The question does not arise here,
rather than being answered somewhere else.

Only the fields present are changed; a field that is absent is left alone.

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/users`.

Returns **every** account, with no row-level scope. G1 was answered on
2026-09-14: administration is an out-of-game function, so a role holding `read`
on `/system/users` may read any account. Inside a game a Commando cannot take
administrative action at all, which is a separate concern carried by the
game-scoped policies. See `docs/client-questions.md`.

The Casbin check on the resource family is therefore the whole rule, and no
service method compares the actor's unit against the target's.

item.name: Retire a unit type, and everything beneath it

request.description:
Requires the `retire` action on `/system/unit-types`.

Withdraws the type, every unit class under it, and every hull in those classes — in one
transaction. See `RetirementBlocked` for the one case that refuses this, and `TaxonomyRetirement`
for what comes back.

**THIS REPLACES `DELETE /unit-types/{id}`, AND THAT IS A BEHAVIOUR CHANGE.** The delete was
refused with `409` by the foreign key while any class belonged to the type, so an operator naming
a type that was in use was told no and given no way forward. The retirement cascades instead,
which is what the scope update asked for. A DELETE that withdrew a class's whole hull complement
would also be the most surprising request in the API, which is why the verb changed with it.

**`is_system` DOES NOT BLOCK THIS, and the client must not block it either.** All nineteen
seeded types carry that flag, and it records who AUTHORED a row rather than whether the row may
be withdrawn. A client that disables the affordance on `is_system` rows would make this endpoint
unreachable for every type the fleet actually has. The DELETE this replaces told the frontend
teams the opposite, and that instruction is now withdrawn.

response.name: Retired, with everything that went with it.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/unit-types`.

Every field is optional; only the fields present are changed. `name` cannot be cleared.

**`id_unit_category` is patchable, so a type can be MOVED between categories.** That is a
real edit — the taxonomy is corrected, not only extended — and it is why the merge happens
against the stored row rather than only against what the request named.

**MOVING A TYPE MOVES EVERYTHING UNDER IT.** The category is reached THROUGH the type, so
every class that belongs to this type — and therefore every hull of those classes — changes
category with it. Existing hulls are NOT re-checked against the ownership rule, so a hull whose
branch does not own the new category keeps existing and keeps working; only its next write is
judged. That is deliberate: the rule governs writes, and the alternative is refusing a taxonomy
correction because of hulls the operator never mentioned, with no way forward except editing
those hulls one at a time.

**`is_system` is not patchable.** It records how a row came to exist; a writable flag would let
a seeded type be relabelled into an ordinary one and then deleted.

item.name: Unit types, each with the category it belongs to

query.description:
Only the types belonging to this category. Resolve the id from `/helpers` under
`unit_categories`. Omit for every type in the system.

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/unit-types`.

**The only endpoint that carries the type -> category link.**

`GET /unit-classes` returns each class with its `unit_type`, but that object is the shared
lookup shape, which deliberately carries no parent — so a client holding a class can reach
its **type** and stop there. `unit_types.id_unit_category` exists in the database and is
invisible through `/helpers`, which excludes domain columns so that one column list and one
scan can cover every lookup table.

That made the taxonomy unreachable in one direction: **Kategori could not be resolved from
Tipe or from Kelas by any endpoint.** This one closes the chain, so a breadcrumb
Domain > Kategori > Tipe > Kelas > Aset can be rendered from API data instead of a mapping
hardcoded in the client.

Read-only. Unit types are seeded master data an operator picks from; no route authors them.

## Filtering by category

`?id_unit_category=<id>` returns only the types in that category. Omit it for the whole
taxonomy.

A query parameter rather than a route of its own, for two reasons. These are the same rows
under the same permission, so a second route would need another Casbin object and a new
grant on every role in order to return a subset. And the response shape is unchanged either
way — every entry still carries its `category` — so a client already reading this endpoint
needs no new parsing to use it.

**An id that names no category, and one that holds no types, both return `[]`.** The two
are not distinguished, deliberately: the taxonomy screen draws a row for every category
whether or not it holds anything, and it already has the category list, so an empty result
renders correctly either way rather than being an error to reconcile.

**`?id_unit_category=0` is NOT rejected: it returns the whole taxonomy.** The field is a
plain integer, so zero is indistinguishable from the parameter being absent, and the
`minimum: 1` below is therefore declarative rather than enforced for zero. A client sending
zero sees every type, which reads in the UI as "this category contains everything". Send the
parameter or leave it out; do not send zero.

A NON-NUMERIC value is refused with **422**, not 400.

item.name: Retire a unit category, and everything beneath it

request.description:
Requires the `retire` action on `/system/unit-categories`.

Withdraws the category, its types, their classes and every hull in them — in one transaction.
See `RetirementBlocked` for the one case that refuses this, and `TaxonomyRetirement` for what
comes back.

**READ THE MAGNITUDE BEFORE CALLING THIS.** It is the widest operation in the API. On a register
of 124 hulls it withdraws 25 for Amphibious, 22 for Patrol Craft and 21 for Fast Attack Craft;
the counts come back in the response, but they arrive AFTER the act. The confirmation belongs
in the client, which is why the response is counts rather than `204`.

**THE BRANCH MAPPING GOES WITH IT, AND THAT HAS A CONSEQUENCE.** A branch's claim to a category
that no longer exists is not worth keeping, so those mapping rows are removed. If the category
was a branch's last one then that branch now operates nothing — and because a hull's branch must
own its class's category, **every hull create and update for that branch starts failing**. Check
`GET /unit-categories?id_service_branch=` first, and re-assign the branch afterwards.

That mapping still cascades on a tombstone, which is a change from the hard delete this
replaces: the branch rows are REMOVED rather than pointing at a retired category, so the
ownership rule and the taxonomy cannot disagree about what a branch operates.

**`is_system` DOES NOT BLOCK THIS** — see the note on the unit-type operation for why.

this one (Domain > Kategori > Tipe > Kelas). Resolve the id from `/units/asset-groups`,
where the tab's `id` is this value and its `hull_count` is the number of hulls the same
tab holds in `GET /units`.

**A category with no group (`id_asset_group: null`) is returned by the `Other` group.**
That group is where its hulls are counted, so the `Other` tab lists exactly the

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/unit-categories`.

The KATEGORI column of the taxonomy screen: every category, with how many types sit
DIRECTLY beneath it.

**THE COUNT IS OF THE LEVEL BELOW, NOT OF EVERYTHING BENEATH.** A category reports its
types, a type its classes (`GET /unit-types`), and a class its hulls
(`UnitClassSummary.hull_count`). That is what lets a drill-down add up: the numbers beside
the rows of one column sum to the header count of the next.

**Why this is not a flag on `/helpers`.** `unit_categories` IS served there — but through
the shared lookup shape, which is deliberately one structure across every lookup table. A
per-table `type_count` would make it eleven shapes and force every consumer to know which
one it was holding. A count describes the TAXONOMY rather than the lookup row, so it
belongs on a route that owns the taxonomy.

**No paging.** Ten-odd rows are drawn in full, and a page of a picker is an incomplete
picker.

## Filtering by service branch

`?id_service_branch=<id>` returns only the categories that branch OWNS. Omit it for every
category.

**Ownership is declared, not derived.** Which categories a branch counts is a mapping the
CMS authors, not a query over the hulls that happen to exist — so a branch shows its
categories even while it holds no hulls of that kind. The taxonomy is a plan, and a plan an
empty warehouse cannot express is not much of one.

**A branch that owns nothing, and an id that names no branch, both return `[]`** — the same
deliberately-unhelpful answer as `?id_unit_category` on `/unit-types`, for the same reason:
the screen draws a row per category and an empty list renders correctly, whereas an error
would have to be reconciled.

**`?id_service_branch=0` is NOT rejected: it returns every category.** The field is a plain
integer, so zero is indistinguishable from the parameter being absent, and the
`minimum: 1` below is therefore declarative rather than enforced for zero. A client sending
zero sees the whole taxonomy, which reads in the UI as "this branch owns everything". Send
the parameter or leave it out; do not send zero.

A NON-NUMERIC value is refused with **422**, not 400.

## Authoring

Since migration 000024 the taxonomy is operator-authorable: `POST` here, plus `PATCH` on
`/unit-categories/{id}`. This paragraph used to read "Read-only. Categories are seeded master
data; no route authors them", which was true when it was written.

**THERE IS NO DELETE ANY MORE — `POST /unit-categories/{id}/retirement` REPLACES IT.** Read that
operation before offering the affordance anywhere. It cascades to every type, class and hull
beneath the category, which makes it the widest single request in the API.

**`is_system` IS NOT A RETIREMENT GUARD, and the client must not treat it as one.** Every
category 000002 seeded carries the flag, and it records who AUTHORED a row rather than whether
the row may be withdrawn. This paragraph used to instruct the opposite — "Disable the delete
affordance on `is_system` rows" — and that instruction is WITHDRAWN: following it now would
make the retirement unreachable for all ten categories the fleet actually has.

**The foreign key stopped being a fallback at the same time.** It used to be what refused a
category holding types, and every seeded category is covered by it. A retirement does not
delete, so the constraint never fires — what limits the damage now is the client's own
confirmation and the counts that come back in the response.

**There IS a soft delete, as of migration 000029.** 000019's argument against a tombstone —
that `is_system` already marks what a migration wrote, so a `deleted_at` beside it would be
"a second, quieter way to hide a row" — is reversed there. The reason it no longer holds is that
the VERB changed, not that the note was wrong: a hard delete cannot express a cascade, because
every foreign key in this hierarchy is `NO ACTION` and a category with types under it could not
be deleted at all. The tombstone is not a preference, it is the only mechanism in the schema
that can carry one.

item.name: What a game role may do inside an exercise

request.description:
The role's whole matrix: every `(object, action)` pair it holds.

Requires the `read` action on `/system/game-roles` — the same one that reads the vocabulary,
because the matrix is part of administering it and a separate object would be a second grant
to keep in step with the first.

**A role with no permissions is an ordinary state, not an error.** The role exists, the CMS
draws an empty matrix, and its holders can do nothing in an exercise until rows are added. A
role created through `POST /game-roles` starts exactly here.

## What a game role may hold

`object` is a **game resource** and nothing else. The object is the only thing standing between
a game role and the application surface, because a game role's policies carry the wildcard
domain so that "a Referee may judge" is true in every exercise. Anything outside `/games/` is
refused with `400`. The enum below is the complete set; a pair that is not in it is refused
rather than silently stored.

`action` is likewise narrower than the full action vocabulary. `create` and `delete` are
absent on purpose: a participant is added to a game by UPDATING its roster, not by creating
anything, so a `create` grant would be a checkbox that changes nothing.

## The labels arrive with the pairs

Every entry carries `name`, `id_name`, `description_en` and `description_id` beside the pair —
the same shape `GET /game-permissions` serves — so a matrix screen draws its checkboxes from
THIS response alone. A client neither carries its own copy of the vocabulary, which drifts, nor
fetches the vocabulary separately and joins on every render.

**The two responses answer different questions and both are needed:** `/game-permissions` is
what COULD be granted, this is what IS. They now share one entry shape, so a screen holds the
two lists in a single collection type — and `PUT` accepts entries with the labels present and
ignores them, which means a client may read a matrix and write it straight back.

**A row whose four labels are empty strings** means the pair has left the enforced vocabulary,
which is possible if the list shrank after the grant was written. `object` and `action` still
identify it, and the server logs the drift rather than failing the screen.

item.name: Replace a game role's whole permission matrix

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/game-roles`.

**REPLACE, not merge** — the same shape `PUT /users/{id}/roles` uses, and the verb is the
contract rather than a preference. An additive call would let a permission be granted through
this endpoint but never withdrawn, so the matrix could only ever widen. The revocation is the
security-relevant direction: a policy that outlives the row still passes every in-game check.

**`permissions: []` is a valid request and revokes everything.** It says this role may do
nothing, which is what an operator means when a role exists but should not yet be usable.
OMITTING the field is refused with `400`: "I forgot" and "nothing" must not arrive as the
same request, because reading the first as the second silently strips a role's authority.

## The change takes effect immediately, inside this process

The matrix is written to `game_role_permissions` — the source of truth, with `created_by` and
a tombstone per revoked row — and the authorization engine is then reconciled to it. A policy
store that cannot be reached is **logged and not reported**: the database is the truth and
reporting a failure would tell an operator their change did not happen when it did. The
reconciliation runs again at startup and repairs any gap.

## Refusals

| Condition | Status |
|---|---|
| `object` outside `/games/` | `400`, naming `permissions.<i>.object` |
| `action` not in the vocabulary above | `400`, naming `permissions.<i>.action` |
| the same pair listed twice | `400`, naming `permissions.<i>` |
| `permissions` absent | `400`, naming `permissions` |
| no such role | `404` |

item.name: Delete one of your own game roles

request.description:
Requires the `delete` action on `/system/game-roles`.

**Two refusals, both `409`, and both about the row rather than about the caller.**

1. **A seeded role cannot be deleted.** Its `is_system` is true, and the API refuses — unlike
   the unit taxonomy, where that flag is only a hint. The seeded roles are named by the
   policies that grant in-game authority, so removing one would leave a policy pointing at a
   role that no longer exists. Rename it instead; a rename is safe.
2. **A role any participant holds cannot be deleted.** `game_participants.id_game_role` is
   NO ACTION, so the database refuses rather than cascading — a cascade would silently remove
   people from a live exercise. Remove them from their games first.

**There is no soft delete.** A delete is a delete and the row is gone.

request.description:
Every role a participant can hold in an exercise — Commando, Game Master, Referee, and the
rest of the judge side.

**This is the same eight rows `/helpers` returns under `game_roles`.** The two routes share
one query, which is why they cannot disagree about a column. They are not the same
PERMISSION: `/helpers` asks "may this caller read every lookup table", and this asks "may
this caller read the game-role vocabulary". A client that already reads `/helpers` needs
nothing here for the list; this exists so that authoring has a surface that owns one table.

**`is_judge_side` is the field that matters.** It decides whether a holder is EXCLUDED from
the readiness gate at Preparation. Editing it changes whether an exercise can advance, so a
role that is not judge-side must declare itself ready before the game may be executed.

**No paging.** Eight-odd rows of master data are drawn in full, and a page of a picker is an
incomplete picker.

## TEMPLATES ONLY — the copies belong to a game

Since 2026-09-28 roles are **per game**: the eight rows here are the TEMPLATES an operator
authors and every new exercise is cloned from, and each game owns its own copy of them. **This
route returns the templates; `/games/{id}/roles` returns one game's copies**, and a client
placing a participant must use that one — a role belongs to exactly one game and the database
refuses a participant holding anything else.

**A NAME no longer identifies a row.** `Commando` is nine rows here: one template and one per
game. Uniqueness is per game, so two exercises may each have a `Commando` and neither is the
other's. IDs never overlap between a template and a copy.

**Editing a template does not change an existing game.** The clone is taken at creation and is
independent from then on, because authority is per game: a Referee who may change the time
factor in one exercise does not carry it into another.

## Renaming is safe; deleting a seeded row is not

A rename is a normal edit and nothing needs to be re-synced: the policies that grant in-game
authority are keyed on the role **id**, never its name, so renaming a role cannot revoke what
it grants. See `casbin.GameRoleSubject`. (One name-keyed reader remains — staff visibility in
`GameService` — and it is tracked as B13 in `docs/backlog.md`.)

**A seeded row cannot be deleted, and the API enforces that with `409`.** This differs from
the unit taxonomy, where `is_system` is a signal to the client only. The seeded game roles are
named by the policies that grant in-game authority — deleting the one that grants the state
transition would leave a policy pointing at a role that no longer exists, and no exercise
could ever leave planning again.

A role that any participant holds is refused separately by the foreign key, also with `409`.

item.name: Every permission a game role can be granted

request.description:
The vocabulary itself: every pair a game role may hold, each with the labels a client draws it
with.

Requires the `read` action on `/system/game-roles` — the same gate as the role list, because
this is part of administering the role vocabulary rather than something a participant holds.

## Read this rather than hardcoding the list

The accepted pairs are **enforced by the server**: a grant naming a pair that no route asks for
is refused with `400`. A client carrying its own copy of the list therefore disagrees with the
server the moment one changes, and it disagrees in two different ways — it omits a newly added
permission, and it keeps offering a checkbox whose grant the server refuses.

**That refusal is deliberate, and is not a bug to work around.** An authority nothing enforces is
one the screen reports as held and the server does not honour, so the grantable set is kept to
exactly what this build asks for. This endpoint is how a client learns it — and what it returns
**is** the accepted set, so there is no second list to reconcile.

## The labels are why this endpoint exists at all

`object` and `action` are **codes** — `/games/judgements`, `judge` — and they are what a
`PUT /game-roles/{id}/permissions` sends back. They are not what a Game Master should be shown,
so every pair carries four labels:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | short **English** label — what a checkbox says |
| `id_name` | short **Indonesian** label |
| `description_en` | long English explanation, for a tooltip or a line of help |
| `description_id` | long Indonesian explanation |

**All four are always present and never empty.** The vocabulary is fixed and fully labelled, and
a test enforces it — so an absent or empty label is a server defect rather than a permission
that legitimately has no name, and a client can rely on having something to draw for every row.

## The order is fixed

Pairs come back grouped by resource, in a stable order, so two screens built from this response
lay out identically.

## This is not a role's matrix

`GET /game-roles/{id}/permissions` answers **what a role holds**; this answers **what could be
granted**. A matrix screen reads both — this one to draw the rows, that one to tick them.

response.name: The whole vocabulary, with labels for each pair.

item.name: How many hulls each service branch holds

request.description:
The CMS's top-level inventory tabs: one count per service branch.

**THE COUNT IS OF LIVE HULLS**, which is what the drill-down eventually selects. The taxonomy
counts one level down from each of its own rows — a category counts types, a type counts
classes, a class counts hulls (`UnitClassSummary.hull_count`) — and this is the same idea
applied to the axis across the top of the screen.

**Every branch is returned, including one holding nothing**, so a tab with no hulls renders a
zero rather than a missing number.

**Every live hull is counted exactly once.** `units.id_service_branch` is `NOT NULL`, so the
counts sum to the size of the inventory and there is no unassigned residue for a client to
render as "other". A tab for anything beyond these branches has no data behind it.

## Why this sits under `/units`

The numbers describe HULLS, so it is gated on the `read` action for `/system/units`: whoever
may read the register may read how large it is. A `/service-branches` resource of its own
would have needed a new policy object and a grant on every role, in order to serve rows that
`/helpers` already hands out.

A STATIC SEGMENT BESIDE `GET /units/{id}` IS DELIBERATE AND SAFE, and the routers package
pins that routing property in a test — without it `service-branches` would be read as a hull
id and the caller would get a 400 about a malformed path parameter instead of a count.

request.description:

The count is of LIVE HULLS, and the group is read from the hull's **category**: the client's
own breadcrumb is Domain > Kategori > Tipe > Kelas > Aset, so this rung sits above the
category, and it is stored on the category rather than on the hull.

submarine moves Submerged and is an Aset Laut.

For the reason `GET /units/service-branches` gives: the numbers describe HULLS, so this is
gated on the `read` action for `/system/units`, and no new policy object is invented to serve
a count of rows the caller can already list. The static segment beside `GET /units/{id}` is
safe for the reason `TestStaticSegmentBeatsParam` pins — without it `asset-groups` would be

**THIS IS THE ONLY WAY TO REMOVE A PICTURE, AND IT EXISTS BECAUSE ABSENCE MEANS SOMETHING

unreferenced bytes in the bucket, which cost storage and nothing else; the opposite order would
leave a hull naming an object that is not there, and every read would presign that name into a
URL that 404s. The object delete is best-effort and is logged rather than reported, because
failing the request would tell an operator the picture is still there when the hull no longer
names it.

item.name: Take units out of a hull

request.description:
**DETACHING IS A PHYSICAL DELETE**, and that is not an exception to this API's "no delete near
history": that rule is about an EXERCISE — the fix chain is a position record — while this is register
authoring, the same kind of thing as releasing a piece from a game.

**THE HULL IS NAMED IN THE PATH, WHICH THE SINGLE-UNIT ROUTE DID NOT USE.** A detach used to be
identified by the child alone — one direct host is what makes that possible — so a caller could take a
hull off a ship it had never named. A batch is written from ONE hull's screen: a list of what this ship
carries, with boxes ticked. The hull is therefore known, and every unit in the list is checked to be in
THIS one; a unit that is inside a different hull is refused and **the refusal names the hull it is
actually in**.

**A POST WITH A BODY RATHER THAN A `DELETE` WITH ONE.** The units to remove are a list, and a `DELETE`
carrying a body is dropped by intermediaries often enough to be a hazard — so the action is spelled as
a sub-resource, the way `/games/{id}/transitions` already spells one.

**ALL OF IT OR NONE OF IT**, exactly as on the attach, and the refusals are collected per row as
`unit_ids[<index>]`: a unit that is inside nothing, a unit that is inside a DIFFERENT hull, an id that
names nothing, an id that appears twice. The answer on success is the host's REMAINING contents,
because that is what the caller was looking at.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/units`.

**FIVE REFUSALS AND ONE WARNING, AND THEY ARE ABOUT THE WHOLE REQUEST.**

* A unit **cannot be carried by itself**, cannot be carried by something it carries **directly or
  through another hull** (a ring, which no read could ever finish), and cannot be **already inside
  something else** — a unit has one direct host, and the refusal names the hull it is on so the
  operator can detach it. An id that **names nothing**, or that appears **twice in the list**, is the
  same kind of mistake. All of these are **400**, with a field error per offending row on
  `unit_ids[<index>]`.
* **THE HULL'S PICTURE IS THE HARD CEILING** (2026-10-13, the same day the fit's ceiling landed):
  **an `embarkation` box is a place for one unit**, and its `id_asset_group` decides which kind. A
  request that would put more units of a group aboard than the hull has boxes of that group is a
  **400** naming the rows that do not fit, and NOTHING is written. A unit whose category names no
  asset group cannot be carried by any box, and a hull with no boxes of the group takes nothing of
  it — both with their own sentence, because the fix is different in each case. "No boxes" and "no
  boxes left" are different states: see `GET /units/{id}/slots`.
* A hull named in the PATH that does not exist is **404**. The units are in the body, so an id there
  is payload rather than the resource being addressed, and a payload naming nothing is one of the
  `400`s above.
* Two operators attaching the same unit at the same moment is **409** — the state, not the request.

**ALL OF IT OR NONE OF IT.** The whole list goes into ONE transaction: a request that cannot be
applied in full writes NOTHING. A partly-attached ship would leave the operator looking at a
composition they did not ask for and could not tell apart from the one they did.

**A COMPLEMENT PASSED IS A WARNING, NOT A REFUSAL**, and it is measured over the WHOLE LIST. If the
host has declared how many of a kind it carries and the batch goes past it, the attach HAPPENS and the
answer reports which complement was exceeded and by how much — five helicopters against a complement
of four is one row saying five. An overloaded ship is a scenario rather than a mistake, and a hardness
there would make it unrepresentable.

**THE BOXES ARE NOT THE COMPLEMENT, AND THEY ANSWER DIFFERENTLY ON PURPOSE.** A complement is a PLAN
and a box is a PLACE: a hull with four boxes and a declared complement of two warns at three and
takes four, while a hull with two boxes refuses the third whatever she declares. Both are checked on
this route, the boxes first — and their refusal is the one that names a ROW, because the row is what
the operator removes.

**THE ANSWER IS THE HOST'S CONTENTS**, the same shape the read returns, so a client never has to fetch
what it has just changed.

item.name: The boxes drawn on a unit's picture

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/units`.

**THE BOXES ARE THE CEILING** (client, 2026-10-13). Until migration 000089 a hull's "how many of these
may she take" was a number an operator typed on the register; it is now `COUNT(*)` per kind over these
rows — six weapon boxes mean at most six weapons, and nobody sets a hard limit by hand.

**AN EMPTY PICTURE MEANS MANEUVER ONLY.** A hull with no boxes may be fitted with nothing and may carry
nothing. It fails closed on purpose, matching "no row means no" everywhere in this API.

**THE LABELS TRAVEL WITH THE ROWS** — the asset group's own name, and the default equipment's code and
name — so drawing a picture of twenty boxes is one request rather than twenty-one. A box whose default
equipment has since been retired still reports it: the box is the operator's drawing, and a box that
plainly refers to something but cannot say what is worse than one naming a withdrawn weapon.

item.name: Draw a unit's boxes, as a whole picture

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/units` — deliberately the same action that clears the hull's
own picture: whoever may annotate a ship's photograph is deciding how many weapons that ship can take,
so it must not be an object a Referee could be granted instead.

**THE BODY IS THE WHOLE PICTURE, BECAUSE THE SCREEN ALREADY IS ONE.** The CMS page holds the picture in
a buffer, the operator drags boxes about, and Save sends every box. A box the request does not name has
therefore been REMOVED, and an **empty list means this hull has no boxes at all**.

**SENDING A BOX'S `id` BACK IS WHAT KEEPS IT THE SAME BOX.** An entry with no `id` is a new box; an id
that is not one of this hull's boxes is `400` naming `slots[i].id`, as is the same id sent twice. The
identity is load-bearing rather than tidy: the in-exercise fit remembers which box something sits in
(`id_unit_slot` on the game's equipment fit), and removing a box removes the fits that sat in it — so a
write that regenerated ids would make an ordinary re-save look like the entire picture had been deleted
and replaced, and would empty every fit on the hull.

**REMOVING A BOX A FIT IS SITTING IN IS THE ONE THING HERE THAT READS AN EXERCISE**, and the answer
depends on where that exercise is. While it is still in `planning` the fits in the removed boxes go with
them, because a plan is editable — the count is reported in the log, and the fits are the operator's own
doing. While it is PAST `planning` the whole write is a **409**, naming how many fits are in the way:
the plan is frozen once play begins, so a box an exercise under way is using cannot be taken off the hull
until that exercise is over. Nothing is written in that case, including the boxes the body did name.

**`x` AND `y` ARE REQUIRED** and are fractions of the picture (`0..1`), so a picture served at another
size does not move the boxes. `rotation` defaults to `0` and `scale` to `1`; a full turn is zero, so
`360` is refused rather than accepted as another spelling of it.

**THE TWO SHAPES OF BOX ARE REFUSED BY FIELD.** An embarkation box needs `id_asset_group` and may not
name an equipment; a weapon, mine or sensor box may name an `id_equipment` — its **default equipment** —
and may not carry an asset group. An `embarkation` box's count is also a CEILING: the hull may not be
sent more of an asset group than she has boxes for, on either attach path, and a box an exercise under
way is using cannot be removed at all.

**AND THE DEFAULT IS WHAT A HULL IS SEEDED WITH WHEN SHE JOINS AN EXERCISE** (2026-10-13): every equipment
box carrying one becomes a line of her fit at assignment, while the exercise is still `planning`. That is
the field's purpose, and until that day nothing acted on it — which is why the default is now REFUSED
when the register permits this hull none of that equipment, and refused when it is not a live row of the
box's own kind. **Declare the allowance first, then draw the boxes.** The SEED checks the permission a
second time, because a register can be narrowed after a picture was drawn; a default that has since gone
stale leaves its box without a line and errors nothing.

request.description:
Requires the `create` action on `/system/units`.

**This is not an update.** A new version is appended, the previous one is kept
untouched with `is_current` set false, and games that referenced it continue to see
the numbers the judges actually saw. That is the point of the whole design: a figure
corrected in October must not rewrite a game judged in September.

`version` is **not accepted from the client.** It is assigned by the server as
current + 1. Two operators publishing concurrently would otherwise both choose the
same number, and the difference between "the second is rejected" and "the second
silently overwrites the first" is the difference between a conflict and lost data.
The database's unique index on `(id_unit, version)` rejects the loser, which surfaces
as 409.

Any numeric field may be omitted or sent as `null`, and **null means unknown, not
zero.** The source data carries no submerged speed for any of the four submarines;
treating a missing value as zero would freeze the vessel, and as unbounded would let
it outrun a frigate. A client must decline to compute movement from a value it does
not have, and say so — the generated clients enforce this by making the field a
pointer.

If `turn_rate_max_deg_s` is omitted, the class's `default_turn_rate_max_deg_s` is
used and `turn_rate_is_derived` is set true, marking it as an estimate the CMS can
flag. Supplying a value sets it false, recording that a person asserted it.

item.name: List a hull's published speeds, one entry per medium

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/units`.

**EVERY MEDIUM IN THE VOCABULARY, NOT ONLY THE ONES THIS HULL HOLDS A FIGURE FOR.** The
question a client is really asking is "may this hull be ordered in Land?", and a list that
omitted Land because the hull has no figure would answer it with silence. An entry whose
figures are absent says "no figure" — the same answer the order clamp gives, and the same
refusal.

**THE FIGURES ARE SI — METRES PER SECOND** — because that is how they are stored. `speed_max_kn`
and `speed_cruise_kn` are the same facts converted, and are what a ship's speed is published and
ordered in. The knots are rounded to the hundredth a speed is expressed at, which is the same
rounding the clamp applies to its limit, so a screen and an order cannot disagree about the
number.

**`is_default` MARKS THE MEDIUM AN ORDER THAT NAMES NONE IS JUDGED IN** — the hull's own movement
domain, when that is also a medium. **NO ENTRY IS MARKED FOR AN AMPHIBIOUS HULL**, because
`Amphibious` is a kind of mover rather than something to move through: such a hull drives on land
and swims on the surface, and an order must say which.

**THIS IS NOT `/specifications`.** A specification is an append-only version with a history a game
can cite; a speed belongs to the hull and has none, which is why 000072 moved it out. It is also
**the same table the order clamp reads**, so the two cannot drift — see
`POST /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/order`.

The vocabulary is served here rather than through `/helpers` on purpose: that endpoint is a picker
over the shared lookup shape, and `movement_media` deliberately is not one — a second list that
looks like `movement_domains` is a confusion the register already warns about.

item.name: Replace a hull's published speeds, one entry per medium

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/units`.

**A REPLACE, NOT A MERGE.** A medium the request does not name holds NO figure afterwards, and an
empty list clears them all — following `PUT /units/{id}/capacities`, and for the reason given there:
a half-applied set is a fleet nobody can read. It is also the only shape the storage permits, since a
row with neither a maximum nor a cruise is not a state `unit_speeds` can hold.

**SI ONLY — metres per second.** That is the unit the figures are STORED in, so this is the one
direction in this API where nobody converts; the knots come back derived, rounded to the hundredth a
speed is expressed at. Accepting knots as well would be a second way to say one fact, and the value
could not round-trip, because the column is not in knots.

**THIS IS NOW THE ONLY WAY A SPEED IS SET.** Until 000073 the three `speed_*_kn` fields on
`POST /units/{id}/specifications` carried them as well, and because that path mirrored the whole set
on every publish, correcting a hull's BEAM would have deleted a speed set here and rebuilt it from a
stale column.

A medium the vocabulary does not have is a **400 naming it**, as is a medium named twice. A row that
carries NEITHER figure is accepted, and has the same effect as leaving it out: the request is a
whole-set replacement, so the two say one thing.

request.description:
Closes the vessel's current assignment and opens a new one **in a single transaction**.

The two writes cannot be separated. Between them the vessel has no commander, and if the
second failed it would be left uncommanded with nobody told — which is why there is one
operation here rather than separate "clear" and "set" calls whose order a caller could get
wrong.

vessel, in the same way a hull's picture is a field of a hull and is gated on `/system/units`.
The feed object itself is read-only, and nothing here writes through it.

An unknown `id_user` is a **400 naming the field**, not a 404: the resource in the path
exists, and it is the body that names a user who does not.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/units`.

Every field is optional; only the fields present are changed.

To **remove** a hull number, send an **empty string**, not `null`. An explicit
`null` cannot be used to clear anything: OpenAPI 3.0 cannot distinguish a field
absent from a field explicitly null, so a generated client renders both as a nil
pointer with `omitempty` and sends neither. See the note on PATCH and nullable
fields at the top of this document.

`commissioned_year_from` and `commissioned_year_to` **cannot be cleared at all**
in this version. They are nullable, but the empty-string convention is
unavailable for an integer and `0` is below the permitted minimum, so a year
entered wrongly can be corrected to another year but not back to unknown.
Recorded rather than fixed because the fix changes the wire format and therefore
both generated clients.

Changing `id_unit_class` changes the hull's type, and therefore its category,
because classification lives on the class. Existing specification versions are
**not** re-validated against the new class: they record what was published at the
time, and rewriting them to match a later taxonomy change is exactly what the
append-only design exists to prevent.

**Either field of the branch/class pair may be changed alone, and the ownership rule is
re-checked against the MERGED pair.** Moving a hull to a class its branch does not operate,
or to a branch that does not operate its class, is refused with `400` and
`data.errors.id_service_branch` — the rule `POST /units` applies, evaluated after the merge
rather than against whatever this request happened to name. A check of the request's own
fields would let a single-field PATCH reach a combination the rule forbids.

fleet-register importer, which is deferred. So `GET /units` returning `[]` means nobody has
created anything yet.

The hull's fields as a JSON document — the schema is
`#/components/schemas/UnitCreateRequest`.

The hull's picture. **OPTIONAL** — a hull may be registered before anybody has
photographed it. PNG or JPEG, at most 5 MiB, and the declared `Content-Type` is not

request.description:
Requires the `create` action on `/system/units`.

`name` is unique among live hulls, case-insensitively, and `hull_number` is unique
among live hulls when present. Both rules are **partial** — they apply only to rows
with `deleted_at IS NULL`, so retiring a hull releases its name for a later
generation. Two live hulls may not share a name; a live hull and a retired one may.

This is what makes the source workbook's duplicate row fail loudly instead of
loading a phantom ship: `KRI Lumba-Lumba` appears twice, both with hull `858`.

## The branch must own the class's category

`id_service_branch` must name a service branch that owns the category `id_unit_class`
belongs to. The chain is fixed by the schema — a class belongs to a type, the type to a
category, and a branch owns categories through an operator-authored mapping — so the two
fields in a create body are not independent.

**Refused with `400` and `data.errors.id_service_branch`**, and the message names the CLASS
rather than the category: the client chose the class and never sees a category, so a message
about one would be unactionable.

The mapping is DECLARED rather than derived from the fleet, so the rule holds for a branch
that currently has no hulls. Today every seeded category belongs to `Navy`, which means a
hull for `Army` or `Air Force` is refused until that branch is given a category of its own
— see `GET /unit-categories?id_service_branch=`.

The hull has **no specification** until one is published — see
`POST /units/{id}/specifications`. An engine cannot move a hull with no known
speed, and the API does not invent one.

## And she has NO BOXES

**A NEW HULL'S PICTURE IS EMPTY, AND NOTHING INVENTS BOXES FOR HER** (2026-10-13). Since the boxes are
the ceiling on what a hull may be fitted with and on what she may carry inside her, an un-drawn hull
can be given nothing and takes nothing — `GET /units/{id}/slots` answers `{"slots": []}` until somebody
draws one with `PUT /units/{id}/slots`.

**THIS IS DELIBERATE AND IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING BEFORE THE FIRST IMPORT.** There is no
inheritance from the class, the type or the category: a picture belongs to a SHIP, so ten hulls of one
class are ten pictures to draw. Retiring and re-creating a hull loses hers; an import leaves every hull
it writes with none. A hull with no boxes is not broken — she manoeuvres and carries nothing — but she
IS inert until her picture exists, and that is the state of the whole fleet today.

item.name: What the archive contains, without the pictures

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/units`.

The cheap half of the pair. Call this first, compare the `ETag` against the copy
already held, and download the archive only when something changed — so the common
case is a 304 and no image bytes cross the wire at all.

Its `data` is the same value as the `manifest.json` embedded in the archive, built
once and used by both. They therefore cannot disagree about what was shipped, which
they could if each endpoint assembled its own.

`units_without_image_count` counts the live HULLS that still need a picture. It is
present so that "this hull has no picture" is something the client is TOLD, rather
than something it infers from an absence it cannot distinguish from a failed
download.

IT IS A COUNT AND NOT A LIST, which is the one shape change this archive took on
being repointed. A taxonomy holds a handful of classes, so listing the ones without a
picture cost nothing; an inventory holds thousands of hulls, and that list would be
most of the fleet. `/units` has the names.

item.name: Download every hull picture as one archive

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/units`. The pictures ARE hull data — each belongs to
an individual ship, and the inventory screen is where it is managed — so they share the
hull's permission rather than having one of their own: a separate object would let the two
drift into "you may edit a hull but not its picture", which reads as a CMS bug rather than
as a policy decision.

**These routes used to share `/system/unit-classes`, and the change is the point rather
than a detail.** While the archive held CLASS pictures, the taxonomy was the honest grant.
Now that it holds a photograph of each ship, a policy keyed on the taxonomy would let an
operator read the whole fleet's imagery through a permission that never mentioned a ship.
Nothing replaces the retired class grant: a hull's picture is a FIELD of the hull, set by
editing the hull, so it already travels under `update` on `/system/units`.

**This is the one response in the document that is NOT the standard envelope.**
It is a binary zip: a client either saves it or unzips it, and neither can do
anything with a `data` wrapper around a zip.

The archive holds `manifest.json` FIRST — so it can be read from a stream without
buffering the whole archive or seeking to its end — followed by one entry per HULL
that has a picture.

## Caching

The `ETag` changes when, and only when, the CONTENT changes. Send it back as
`If-None-Match` and the usual answer is `304 Not Modified`, costing no image bytes
at all. Prefer `GET /assets/unit-images/manifest` for the check itself: it
carries the same ETag and weighs a few kilobytes.

Compare the tag, not the clock. HTTP `Date` has one-second resolution, so a
refresh landing in the same second as the previous one would appear unchanged.

item.name: Move a game to another state

request.description:
Authorised by being **this game's Game Master**, not by an application permission.

The route itself carries no permission middleware, so any authenticated caller can REACH it
and only the game's own Game Master is obeyed. That is a widening of who may ask and a
narrowing of who is answered: before participants existed, an administrator was the only
caller who could get here, and any administrator could run any game.

That distinction is the whole reason this is not a `PATCH` on the game. Creating a game is
an application capability — an operator holds `create` on `/system/games` — while running
one is in-game authority, which comes from a participant assignment and is scoped to a
single game. A Casbin object cannot express "the Game Master of THIS game", so the check
is an instance comparison in the service, and a failure is **403, not 404**.

Forward-only, one step at a time:

| From | To | Precondition |
|------|----|--------------|
| `planning` | `preparation` | none — the Game Master decides planning is done |
| `preparation` | `execution` | at least one unit assigned, every unit placed, at least one participant on the exercise side, every one of them ready, and a complete planned window |

**A `fast` game is excused ONE of those five**, and only one: the readiness declaration. The
four that remain are about the PLAN — the window, an assigned force, the placements and
somebody commanding it — and a fast exercise is still an exercise. `pace` is on the game and
editable while it is in `planning`.
| `execution` | `closure` | none — the Game Master ends the exercise |

Judges are excluded from the readiness precondition, which is also what makes B5's
"more lenient readiness gate" for Static a statement about a baseline rather than a new
mechanism.

**The gate has five parts, and the last four are the ones that are easy to leave out.** An
exercise that is READY but has no hulls assigned has nothing to manoeuvre, nothing to give an
order to, and no unit for a Commando to lead. A roster of nothing but Judges satisfies
"everyone is ready" vacuously. A hull with no placement reaches `execution` with no origin
fix, and because the fix chain is append-only it can never be given one — so it would be
visible to the Game Master and impossible to move. And a game with an incomplete planned
window has no declared finish time: a movement model with no clock cannot run, and a track
with no assumed time cannot be replayed.

The refusal names every missing ingredient at once, under `data.errors`, rather than the
first one found — a freshly created game is missing several, and reporting one per attempt
would make the Game Master press Advance twice to learn two things. The backend supplies no
default for either end, so the window is a declaration the Game Master makes rather than a
value the API invents on their behalf.

Note also that a **role change clears readiness**, so a game can be refused by a declaration
the caller did not withdraw.

A skipped step, a step backwards, or a step out of a game already in `closure`, is
**409**. Reporting it as a 400 would suggest the request was malformed; it was well-formed
and refused.

**CLOSING STOPS THE CLOCK, AND SHUTS THE DOORS.** The move writes a zero-rate segment to the
clock and clears `accepting_actions`, in the same transaction as the state — so the exercise's
assumed instant is **frozen at the moment it closed**, everything derived from it stops
changing, and no further order is accepted. Until 2026-10-08 only the state was written: the
clock is a series of segments and this transition wrote none, so the last segment's rate ran
on and a closed exercise went on simulating. A client reading the plot at "now" — `GET
/games/{id}/positions` with no `at` — drew a fleet still under way, and the older rehearsal
exercises had steamed for years.

can tell the exercise's end from a Game Master's stop — the distinction the closed vocabulary
on `time_factor_change.source` exists for. The move publishes **no** `game.clock_changed`:
that event is pause, resume and rate change and a closure is none of the three; the state
change is what a client watches, and the position stream's `final: true` snapshot is what
tells it the plot has stopped.

**A closed exercise has no scenario time after the moment it closed** — the consequence worth
stating, because the frozen instant is what every later read integrates to: a replay seeking
beyond the end shows the end rather than inventing a leg nobody ordered. `closure` is the last
rung of the ladder and `Next()` has no next state from it, so nothing reopens an exercise that
was closed.

request.description:
Requires staff access to the exercise — see the **games** tag for what that means — **or** a game
role holding `read` on `/games/equipment` in this game. Readable at every state, like the roster
and the pieces: reading is not an edit.

**WHAT A HULL CARRIES VERSUS WHAT IT MAY CARRY.** The CMS authors a REGISTER — what a hull may be
given, at four levels (hull, class, type, category) with a maximum per row, on
`/weapons/{id}/allowances` and its siblings. This is the other half: what the Game Master CHOSE for
one hull in this exercise, from that permission. "May carry" and "carries" answer different
questions, and an exercise can say "these, and not those" without editing the fleet.

**EVERY ROW CARRIES A BOX AND A PERMISSION, AND SINCE 2026-10-13 IT CARRIES NO NUMBER AT ALL.** A fit
is one line per BOX drawn on the hull's picture: `id_unit_slot` says which box, and the boxes ARE the
ceiling — six weapon boxes mean at most six weapons, which is what replaced the register's
`max_quantity` (see `EquipmentAllowanceRow`). `allowed` is the register's PERMISSION for this hull,
resolved through its nearest-declaration-wins ladder — the hull's own row first, then its class's, its
type's, its category's.

**`allowed: null` MEANS THE REGISTER PERMITS THIS HULL NONE OF IT**, and it is worth SHOWING rather
than hiding: a fit is a record rather than a permission, so it can outlive the declaration that covered
it — at which point a screen says "carried, and no longer permitted" and an operator fixes the
register. Nothing is corrected for the operator here, unlike on the write, which refuses an entry the
register permits none of.

**WHAT HAPPENS TO A FIT WHEN ITS BOX IS REMOVED IS THE BOX WRITE'S BUSINESS, NOT THIS ONE'S**: a box
removed while the exercise is still in `planning` takes its fits with it, and a box an exercise that
has started is using cannot be removed at all — see `PUT /units/{id}/slots`.

`code` is null when the operator never gave the catalogue entry one. Ordered by kind, then name,
then id, so a screen groups by kind without sorting.

A `unit_id` that is not in this game is a **404**, not an empty list: "this hull was given nothing"
and "there is no such hull" are different answers, and only one of them is fixed by adding
equipment.

Requires staff access to the exercise — see the **games** tag for what that means — **or** a game
role holding `update` on `/games/equipment` in this game. **The game must be in `planning`**;
anything later is a 409.

**PLANNING ONLY, AND THE WINDOW IS THE CLAMP'S OWN.** When a maximum changes under an exercise that
has already begun, the register's write LEAVES THAT EXERCISE ALONE and reports how many fits it
could not reach, because a plan is frozen once play begins. A route open later would let a Game
Master do by hand exactly what the clamp refuses to do.

**THE BODY IS THE WHOLE FIT** — hence `PUT`, which is idempotent. `equipment` may be **absent or
empty**, and that is meaningful rather than a missing value: it says this hull carries none of
anything, which is the only way to say "and not those" after a maximum changes. A `PATCH` would
need a second route for the same statement.

**EVERY LINE NAMES A BOX ON THE HULL'S PICTURE, AND EVERY LINE IS CHECKED.**
`equipment[i].id_unit_slot` must be a box on this hull — the boxes are drawn by the CMS, through
`PUT /units/{id}/slots`, and this is where a fit is put in them. **READ WHICH BOXES EXIST FROM
`GET /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/slots`**, NOT from the CMS route: that one needs `/system/units` read,
which a game role cannot hold, and the game-scoped read returns the same list under this object's own
permission. `equipment[i].id_equipment` must be
an entry the register permits this hull, and its KIND must match the box's: a weapon in a mine box is a
400 naming `equipment[i].id_equipment`, since the box's kind is what the check is against. Naming one
box twice is a 400 naming `equipment[i].id_unit_slot`, because a box holds one thing — where the old
shape refused the same EQUIPMENT twice, because a hull then had one quantity of something.

**A HULL WITH NO BOXES CAN BE GIVEN NOTHING**, which is B56's fail-closed rule rather than a gap: with
no boxes a hull maneuvers and that is all, so the refusal is a 400 naming `equipment[i].id_unit_slot`
with a message that says so.

**THE BODY HAS NO NUMBER IN IT AT ALL.** `quantity` is gone rather than defaulted, because "how many"
is now "how many boxes", and the picture already says. A client that still sends one is not refused for
it — unknown properties are ignored — but it decides nothing.

A hull that is not a piece of this game is a **404** before any of this runs, and the composite
foreign key in 000091 makes a fit naming another game's box unrepresentable.

Replacing a fit REPLACES it: a box left out of the body is no longer filled. The write and the
read back are one transaction, and the response is read through the same ladder the `GET` uses, so
a client never sees a different permission than the next read will show.

item.name: List the boxes drawn on a hull's picture, from inside an exercise

request.description:
Requires staff access to the exercise — see the **games** tag for what that means — **or** a game
role holding `read` on `/games/equipment` in this game. Readable at every state, like the fit itself:
reading is not an edit.

**WHY THIS EXISTS, AND IT IS NOT A CONVENIENCE.** A fit line NAMES A BOX: `equipment[i].id_unit_slot`
must be one of this hull's boxes, and naming one twice is a refusal — see
`PUT /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/equipment`. So a caller setting a fit has to know which boxes the
hull has. The route that answers that is `GET /units/{id}/slots`, which is the **CMS's** and requires
`/system/units` read, an APPLICATION permission. **A GAME ROLE CAN NEVER HOLD ONE**: the objects a
game role may be granted are a closed set of `/games/*` — a grant naming `/system/units` is refused
outright — so the two routes cannot be substituted for one another. Without this endpoint a Game
Master granted exactly the capability the fit was built for could be trusted to set one and could not
find out what to put in it.

**THE ALTERNATIVE WAS TO WIDEN THE CMS ROUTE TO ACCEPT THIS PERMISSION TOO**, and that is refused for
a reason worth stating: `/units/{id}/slots` carries no game in its path, so there is nothing to
resolve a game role's grant against and no way to stop a caller holding ONE exercise's `read` from
reading the whole fleet's pictures. Scoping the read by game is what makes the permission mean what it
says — so a hull that is not a piece of THIS game is a **404**, never another exercise's picture.

**THE ANSWER IS THE SAME ENVELOPE `GET /units/{id}/slots` RETURNS** — a list of boxes with the labels
a screen draws them by, and no more. What is IN each box is the fit's own business and its own route:
folding the two together would make this read answer about the exercise while claiming to be about the
hull.

An empty list is the ordinary answer rather than a fault: it is a hull whose picture nobody has drawn,
and a hull with no boxes can be given nothing and carry nothing (`B56`'s fail-closed rule) — which is
a state, not an error.

variable.description: The host piece's id these units are taken out of.

request.description:
**THE HOST IS CHECKED, WHICH A DETACH MUST BE.** A batch is written from ONE host's screen — a list of
what this ship carries, with boxes ticked — so a piece taken out of a hull the operator is not looking
at would be a change they could not see the result of. A piece that is not inside THIS host is a
**400** naming its row.

**A PIECE THAT LEAVES UNDER WAY IS GIVEN A POSITION OF ITS OWN.** A contained unit has no position of
its own — it follows its host's — and the act that lets it go is the only one that can say where it
now is: `PUT /placement` is bound to the setup window and `PUT /position` is refused by a `maneuver`
exercise. So the departing piece gets a fix at **its host's position, its host's heading and its
host's speed** — a boat lowered from a ship making twelve knots is making twelve knots — and it runs
on that until its commander orders something else. In a `static` exercise the same act records a
position with no voyage in it, because there are no voyages in that mode.

**A PIECE THAT ALREADY HAS LEGS OF ITS OWN IS MOVED FROM THE HOST ANYWAY** (2026-10-06). It was
placed before the exercise began, or an earlier departure gave it a place — and while its host HELD
it, that position was never being used: a held piece is not drawn on the plot at all, so its own
chain is history rather than a place. Leaving the stale leg alone would therefore not have preserved
the operator's earlier choice; it would have **teleported the piece onto its pre-exercise mooring at
the instant of release**, possibly hundreds of miles astern of the ship that carried it. So the
departure is always written from the host, and the earlier legs stay in the chain, undrawn.

**THE FIX'S `kind` IS `launch`**, which is a leg nobody ordered — or a `jump`, in a `static`
exercise, where a departure and a drag are the same movement. Either way the row carries
**`id_host`**, the hull the piece came from, and that is what a client reads to tell a departure from
an order or a drag. It IS on the timeline, in the `order` stream: see `GET /games/{id}/timeline`,
which is also the only place that fact is recorded, because a detach deletes the embarkation row.

request.description:
**THE HOST LETS A UNIT GO**, which is the client's rule read exactly: a unit inside another "takes no
orders — in the game, until the host clears it". Clearing is the whole of that permission.

**WHAT IT CHANGES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT.** A cleared piece may take orders and has a position of its
own — so the readiness gate asks for a placement for it, and a departure under way gives it one. A
cleared piece is STILL INSIDE ITS HOST for everything else: the message chain still reaches it, it is
still obliged to declare ready for a step that relates its host, and releasing the host is still
refused while it is aboard. Clearing a helicopter does not take it off the ship.

**THE AUTHORS ARE THE HOST'S COMMANDER AND ANYBODY WHO MAY EDIT THE FORCE.** "The host lets it go" is
a fact about one hull, and no Casbin object can name a hull — so this route carries no in-game
permission and the service decides, exactly as `/order`, `/movement-mode` and `/position` do.

**THE DEPARTURE'S LEG CARRIES THE HOST'S HEADING AND SPEED**, so a piece that is let go under way
appears where its host is and moving as its host is moving. A piece that already had a position of its
own keeps it.

**ASKING FOR WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE CHANGES NOTHING** and is not an error: it writes no second position,
and the answer is the host's contents either way.

request.description:
**UNITS INSIDE UNITS, AND THIS IS THE EXERCISE'S OWN COMPOSITION.** The CMS says what the fleet MAY
carry; an exercise takes its own copy when a hull is assigned, so a detach in the CMS under a game
under way cannot change who declares ready for the step being played or who a telegram reaches — and
an exercise can say "these, and not those" without touching the fleet.

**`is_cleared` IS THE HOST'S PERMISSION.** A unit inside another takes no orders of its own and has no
position of its own until the host lets it go; `cleared_at` says when that happened, who did it, and

scenario rather than a mistake.

variable.description: The hull's id — the unit's own id, not a game_units row id.

request.description:
**THE ONE GAME ROUTE THAT IS NOT GATED BY A PAIR OF PERMISSIONS.** It accepts an authenticated
caller, and the service then allows THREE kinds of caller:

- **the Commando who commands THIS hull** — the ordinary case, because the crew is who discovers
  that a handset is running, and requiring a Game Master to relay a fact they cannot observe
  would put a person in the path of it. This is an **instance** comparison, which is why it
  cannot be a route gate: a Casbin object names a resource family and carries no instance id.
- a caller with `update` on `/games/units` **in this game**, through a game role an operator
  granted — see the **games** tag;
- an application Administrator, who reaches inside any exercise without being on its roster.

Anybody else receives **403**, not 404: the hull exists and the caller may already have seen it
in a list, so a blocked act reported as "not found" would leave nothing in the record to say
anybody tried.

**THE ONLY PIECE WRITE NOT BOUND TO THE SETUP WINDOW.** Placement, the task organisation and
the crew list all describe the force the exercise was *set up* with, and those answers freeze
once play begins. A movement mode is a different kind of fact: it says what is happening
**now**. A vessel's beacon comes online mid-exercise and goes offline again, so a mode that
could only be declared while planning would be unusable at the one moment it matters. There is
therefore **no state refusal here** — see below for what that means at `closure`.

`auto` means the vessel's own device authors its movement, so
`POST /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/order` refuses with **409**. `manual` is the ordinary case,
and what every piece is until somebody says otherwise.

**`auto` CHANGES WHERE THE POSITION COMES FROM, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THE MODE.** Nobody
steers the hull, so there is no leg to derive a position from: the plot serves the newest
measurement the vessel's device reported at or before the instant asked about, `?at=` playback
included. A device pushes its reports through `POST /live-feed/fixes` at its own interval;
nothing on the server ticks for it. See README §13.

Every plotted row says which it is — `movement_mode` beside `source`, where `auto` + `derived`
means **a device that has said nothing yet** and the hull is drawn at its origin. A measured row
is never clamped and reports `false` rather than inheriting the leg's flag.

**SETTING THE MODE IT ALREADY HAS IS ACCEPTED AND RECORDED**, in the same way a second pause
is: the history records what the Game Master did, and they did it.

**AND IT IS SETTABLE AT `closure`**, which is the consequence of having no window rather than
a decision of its own. Nothing is moved by it — no order is accepted at `closure` in any case
— and what it changes is what a later reader understands about why a hull has no legs after
its origin.

request.description:
Authentication only, with the authority check in the service: **the caller must be this
hull's commander**. That is an instance comparison over a row — an in-game fact, not an
application permission — so no Casbin object appears here, following
`POST /live-feed/fixes`'s shape. The refusal is **403**, not 404, so a blocked order stays
visible in the audit trail.

**A COMMANDO CAN ONLY STEER THEIR OWN HULL.** The hull is in the path because it is the
resource being ordered, but the caller's authority is implied by it: nobody may order a hull
they do not command, and the Game Master who runs the exercise commands no ship in it.

The game must be in `execution`, and must be **accepting actions**. The two are separate
refusals: a game in `planning` has not begun, while a paused one has begun and been stopped.

**AN ORDER IS CLAMPED, NOT REFUSED.** The speed is reduced to the hull's maximum for the
**MEDIUM the order is judged in** — the one `medium` names, or the hull's own movement domain
when it names none — and what the caller asked for is returned as `requested_speed_kn` with
`clamped: true`. A client with a slider is not trusted, but an operator whose slider sat one
notch high should lose the excess speed rather than the whole order — the heading is applied
either way.

**`medium` IS HOW A HULL WITH TWO SPEEDS IS TOLD WHICH ONE APPLIES.** A hull whose movement
domain is `Amphibious` has no medium of that name: it drives on land and swims on the surface,
and those are two different published speeds. It is therefore **refused until the order names
one** — which is the design rather than a gap, because there is no honest default between the
two.

**A HULL WHOSE SPEED CANNOT BE BOUNDED IS REFUSED**, with 409 rather than an unclamped order.
That happens for a hull with no published maximum in the medium it is being ordered in: an
aircraft or a ground formation has none, an amphibious hull asked without a medium has none,
and a hull whose specification nobody has filled in has none either. **In the current fleet
this also means a submarine cannot be ordered to move submerged**, because the imported
specifications give submarines a surfaced maximum only — a data gap surfacing as a refusal
rather than as an unbounded boat. The detail names the medium when the caller named one,
because "no figure for Snorkel" and "nobody has published this ship's particulars" are
different things to go and fix.

**POSITION AND TIME ARE THE SERVER'S.** The position is derived from the hull's previous leg
and the elapsed assumed time; the instant comes from the scenario clock. Neither is accepted
from the client, which is what stops a Commando placing their ship wherever they liked and
stamping it whenever they liked. A leg is a **straight rhumb line** from that point, on the
ordered heading — see the README's §2.

item.name: Publish a frame of a hull being dragged

variable.description: The hull's id — the unit's own id, not a game_units row id.

request.description:
Publishes **one frame** of a hull being moved by hand, so that every other participant sees it
move while it is being moved. Nothing is recorded: no fix is written, the hull's chain is
untouched, and the frame is superseded by the next position snapshot.

**THE SAME REQUEST AND THE SAME GATES AS `PUT /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/position`** — the mode,
the state, the pause and the authority are asked by the same code — with a different consequence.
A frame shown where a commit would be refused would be a lie the operator then acts on, so the two
routes cannot disagree about who may move what, or when.

**IT IS DESIGNED TO BE CALLED REPEATEDLY.** A client sends frames while somebody drags, throttled to
roughly ten a second, and it is the cheapest route in this family: the game and the hull are read,
the authority check for a hull's own commander is in-memory, and nothing is written. It is **not**
the animation source — `game:<id>:positions` carries a snapshot every second and clients interpolate
between two of them (see `docs/movement-formula.md`) — so its job is to shorten the worst case from
one second to a tenth, and a client that skipped it entirely would still draw a correct board, one
tick late.

**IT IS ADVISORY, NOT AUTHORITATIVE.** The frame says where a pointer is; the hull is where the
committed drag put it, and that arrives as `game.hull_jumped` on `game:<id>`. A client that held a
frame as truth would show a hull somewhere the exercise's record does not — and because the frame is
**ephemeral**, an abandoned drag (the pointer left the map, the browser closed) corrects itself
within one snapshot. There is no cleanup protocol and no server-side drag state.

**THIS ROUTE IS WHY CLIENTS DO NOT PUBLISH FOR THEMSELVES.** Centrifugo's `game` namespace does not
enable client publish, so a frame cannot reach participants without passing these gates. If it did,
any participant could broadcast any hull — an opponent's included — wherever they liked, past the
pause and past the mode, on a channel every participant subscribes to.

**THE COMMIT IS THE RECORD.** Draw the frame; do not store it.

response.name: The frame that was published, so the caller sees exactly what everybody else saw.

item.name: Set where a hull is, in a static exercise

variable.description: The hull's id — the unit's own id, not a game_units row id.

request.description:
Sets a hull's position by hand, in an exercise whose `mode` is `static`. The hull stays there
until it is set again — a static exercise has no movement model, so nothing carries a hull on
from where it was put.

**THIS IS THE MIRROR OF `PUT /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/order`, AND THE TWO EXERCISES REFUSE
EACH OTHER'S.** An order states a heading and a speed, which the server integrates over assumed
time; that is a claim about a voyage, and a static exercise has no voyage in it. A drag states a
position; that is a hull being somewhere, and a maneuver exercise derives every hull's position
from its own chain of orders — so accepting one there would move a hull **past the movement
model**, and the track would show a hull covering forty miles in no time at all with nothing
recording how.

| | this route | `PUT .../order` |
|---|---|---|
| input | `latitude`, `longitude` | `heading_deg`, `speed_kn` |
| recorded as | a **jump** (`kind: jump`) | a **leg** (`kind: leg`) |
| accepted in | `static` only | every mode **except** `static` |
| authority | the hull's commander **or** a caller who may edit the force | the hull's commander only |

**THE POSITION IS THE CLIENT'S HERE, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF AN ORDER.** An order refuses a
position because a Commando must not be able to put their ship wherever they like; a drag
accepts one because setting the position **is** the operation. No heading and no speed are
accepted either, for the mirror of that reason: a hull that was set is stationary, and a course
would be one the server has no voyage to advance along.

**THE INSTANT IS THE SERVER'S** — the same scenario clock `GET /games/{id}/clock` reports — so a
client cannot stamp a drag anywhere in the timeline.

**A HULL'S OWN `movement_mode` IS NOT CONSULTED.** An order is refused on an `auto` hull because
its crew cannot take orders; a drag is not an order, and in a static exercise it is the only way
a position can enter at all, since device reports are refused there. Refusing a drag on an `auto`
hull would leave a hull that nothing can move.

The response is the **fix** that was written, whose `kind` is `jump`, so a client learns the
instant the server actually used — the same record an order returns.

response.name: The jump that was recorded.
