item.name: Report where a hull is, within one exercise

variable.description: The hull's id — the unit's own id, not a game_units row id.

request.description:
A device aboard a device-driven hull reports its position **in this exercise**. The hull's
`movement_mode` must be `auto`, and the caller must command that hull **in this game**.

**THE EXERCISE MUST NOT BE `static`**, and that refusal is asked **before** the hull's own
`movement_mode`: a static exercise has no movement model — its positions are set by hand with
`PUT /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/position` — so a device is not a source of truth in one, and
the plot never reads these rows for that game. Ordering the two matters for the answer a caller
gets: a hull in a static exercise is not reporting whatever its own mode says, so telling a
Commando to declare their hull device-driven would be advice that could not make their next
request work. A game's `mode` is fixed once the game LEAVES `planning` — it may be corrected
with `PATCH /games/{id}` while the game is still being planned.

**THIS IS NOT `POST /live-feed/fixes`, AND IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT FEED IT.** The two record
different kinds of fact:

| | this route | `POST /live-feed/fixes` |
|---|---|---|
| what the record is about | a **hull in one exercise** | a **real vessel**, in no game |
| scoped by | `id_game` + `id_unit` | `id_unit` alone |
| may be simulated | **yes** — a simulator, or somebody playing a part | no |
| written to by the other | never | never |

An exercise is allowed to contain fiction; the real-asset picture is not. So a report here
**never** reaches `unit_position_log` or `unit_positions_latest`, and a member of the fleet
reporting through the live feed never appears in an exercise's plot. That is why a crew reporting
here needs **no** vessel-level command (`PUT /units/{id}/commander`), which the feed's instance
check does require: the authority here is the exercise's own hull commander.

**`GET /games/{id}/positions` SERVES THESE.** For a hull in `auto`, the plot draws the newest
report at or before the instant asked about — `?at=` playback included — and every plotted row
says whether its position was `derived` or `measured`. A hull in `auto` that has reported nothing
yet is drawn at its origin and says `derived`, which is what `movement_mode` beside `source` is
there to distinguish.

**THE BATCH IS THE FEED'S SHAPE, ON PURPOSE.** The per-fix fields and their validation are
identical, and the answer carries the same `accepted`/`rejected` counts: the two routes differ in
what the record is ABOUT, not in what a fix looks like. A fix older than the retention window is
**permanently** invalid, so a batch of only such fixes is still a **200** — the counts are the
answer, and there is nothing for the client to retry.

item.name: Put a unit into a game

request.description:
Requires staff access to the exercise — see the **games** tag for what that means — **or**
a game role holding `update` on `/games/units` in this game. The game must be in `planning` or
`preparation`.

**`id_commander` IS REQUIRED**, and that is the rule rather than a convenience. Concept
`[1.7]` defines a game piece as "the 'Game Piece' that will be commanded by the Commando
assigned to it", so a hull with nobody to steer it is not a piece at all — there is no state
in which a unit is in an exercise and nobody commands it. It is also why "a game needs at
least 1 unit and 1 commando" is **one condition in the start gate, not two**.

**The commander must be a participant of THIS game**, which the database enforces through a
composite foreign key rather than trusting this endpoint to remember. 400 naming
`id_commander` otherwise.

**The judge side does not command units.** A Referee "Assesses performance and gives points"
— they run the exercise, they do not take part in it. Refused rather than allowed quietly,
because a piece commanded by a judge is a player wearing a referee's shirt.

**A hull may be in several games at once.** A ship is a real vessel with one hull number; an
exercise is a plan. Uniqueness is per game, so the same hull cannot be listed twice in one
exercise and may appear in as many exercises as the scenario needs.

**SHE ARRIVES WITH WHAT HER PICTURE SAYS SHE CARRIES** (2026-10-13). Assigning a hull also seeds her
equipment fit from the boxes drawn on her photograph: every equipment box with a **default equipment**
becomes one line of the fit, unless the register no longer permits that hull that equipment, in which
case the box keeps its note and the fit records nothing. It is a SEED rather than a standing default —
the GM may empty any box afterwards and it stays empty — and it is the reason a box's default equipment
exists at all.

**IT HAPPENS ONLY WHILE THE GAME IS IN `planning`.** The fit is frozen once play begins, like the rest
of the plan, so a hull assigned in `preparation` arrives holding what her picture said while the exercise
was still being planned — which is to say nothing. That is deliberate rather than a gap: seeding a fit
past planning would do by the back door what the fit's own route refuses by the front.

**AND A HULL WITH NO BOXES ARRIVES WITH NO FIT**, which is every hull until an operator draws her
picture. The boxes are the CMS's own work and nothing invents them: `PUT /units/{id}/slots` is that act.

**409 when that hull is already in this game.**

ready to perform (Via 'Ready Button' or something)".

**SELF-SERVICE, and there is no `id_user` in the request.** The button is pressed by a

— an instance check, not a permission. A body field that must always equal the token's
subject is a field that should not exist.

**409 in two cases**, each with its own reason under `data.errors`:

* the caller's role is on the **judge side**, which the gate exempts. Refused rather than
  accepted-and-ignored: a Referee who pressed Ready, got a 200, and then watched the game
  refuse to advance would reasonably believe the blockage was theirs.
* the game is **not in `preparation`**. Readiness declared while the roster can still change
  under it is premature, and after the gate has been passed it means nothing.

A role change CLEARS readiness — see `PATCH /games/{id}/participants/{user_id}` — so a
client that re-reads its participant row will see `is_ready: false` without having asked.

item.name: The step a participant sees — where the exercise is, what the step says, and what the caller must declare

request.description:
**THE PARTICIPANT'S ONLY DOOR ONTO THE PLAN.** A participant may not read `/games/{id}/scenarios` —
the script is precisely what the people being exercised must not see — so this names the ONE step
whose readiness is being asked for, and nothing about the plan beyond it. The Game Master and the
judges are participants of the exercise they run, so they read this as themselves; an administrator
who is not on the roster has the staff-gated book and readiness reads instead. A caller with no place
in the exercise is refused **403** and not 404: the exercise exists, they may have seen it a moment
ago, and reporting a blocked read as a missing one would hide it from the audit trail.

**`current` IS THE STEP IN PLAY, AND IS ABSENT BETWEEN STEPS** — a state the book has, where the
exercise keeps running while no beat is being played.

**`asking` IS NOT THE STEP IN PLAY, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN.** The gate is asked when the Game
Master presses `Play`, and a replay erases an attempt's declarations with it, so a participant must be
able to declare BEFORE a step starts and AGAIN while nothing is playing. A read tied to the playing
step would be useless at both moments. `asking` therefore names the FIRST step the exercise has NOT
reached, when that step asks this caller at all — and it is **absent** when it does not, rather than
present with a step the caller has no business reading.

**IT IS A HINT; THE DECLARATION ROUTE IS THE AUTHORITY.** `asking` names the step the exercise is next
ON, which is the one the Game Master is about to play — a Game Master who plays out of order makes it
a guess. The declaration route names its step in the path, so a client that knows better may declare
for any step the exercise has not reached; and one that declared for the wrong step has done no harm,
because the gate counts only the step being played.

**`window_end_at` IS AN INSTANT, NOT THE AUTHORED `HHMM`.** The plan states a window as a time of day
on the assumed clock, which is how an author thinks about it; a countdown needs the instant, computed
by the same rule a skip uses. It is absent when the author set no window — a beat with no time on it,
rather than one that ends now.

**THE COUNTS ARE NUMBERS AND NOT NAMES**, deliberately: a commander learns whether they are holding the
step up, and not the composition of the force opposite them. The Game Master's own read —
`GET .../steps/{step_id}/readiness` — is the one that names people.

item.name: What a scenario exercise is holding, for the Game Master or for a Commander

request.description:
**THE PARTICIPANT'S HALF OF THE STAGING RULE.** A `scenario` exercise ACCEPTS an order while no step
that relates the hull is being played and holds it — `POST /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/order`
answers 202 and nothing is drawn — and this is how a client finds out what is waiting, so a
Commander can show it and a Game Master can see what a `Play` is about to release.

**TWO AUDIENCES, ONE ROUTE, AND `scope` SAYS WHICH ONE ANSWERED.** A caller who RUNS the exercise
sees everything it holds (`scope: game`); anybody else sees the orders waiting for the hulls THEY
command (`scope: own`). Neither sees the other's: an order is one person's intention until a beat
makes it a fact.

**A CALLER WHO COMMANDS NOTHING WAITING GETS AN EMPTY LIST RATHER THAN A REFUSAL**, because that is
the honest answer to the question asked — and the exercise's existence is not being concealed by it:
a game that does not exist is a 404 either way.

**NOTHING HERE IS A LEG.** Nothing in this list is on the plot, in the timeline, or derivable as a
position: a held order is a leg that has not happened, and it becomes an ordinary leg at the instant
the beat that releases it names.

request.description:
THE ROLES THIS EXERCISE OWNS — the seats a participant is placed in.

**Not the same list as `/game-roles`.** That route returns the templates the CMS authors; this
returns the copy the game was cloned from them when it was created. Both are eight rows with
the same names, and **their ids do not overlap** — a game's `Commando` is not the template
`Commando`.

**Use this one to fill a seat.** `POST /games/{id}/participants` takes `id_game_role`, and the
role must belong to that game: any other game's role, and any template, is refused with `409`
by the database rather than by a check that could be bypassed.

Roles are per game because authority is: a Referee who may change the time factor in one
exercise does not carry it into another. Editing a role through this game's permission matrix
changes THIS exercise only — see `PUT /game-roles/{id}/permissions`.

**`404` when the game does not exist or has been deleted**, rather than an empty list. An
exercise with no roles is not a state this API produces, so reporting one would send an
operator looking for a bug in the wrong place.

Read by the same people who may fill the roster: the route is gated on the game-participants
object, because a game's roles being private to it is exactly what makes them roster
vocabulary.

a game role holding `update` on `/games/participants` in this game. The game must be in `planning`

**A CALL SIGN IDENTIFIES ONE PERSON ON THE NET.** It is unique within the game and
**case-insensitively** — `alpha-1` and `ALPHA-1` are the same sign, and the second is
refused with a 400 naming `call_sign`, because over a radio the two sound identical and two
people answering to one name is the failure the uniqueness rule exists to prevent. Setting
the sign a participant already holds IS allowed: that is how a client corrects the
capitalisation, and it is not a conflict with itself.

**IT DOES NOT CLEAR READINESS**, which is why it is an endpoint of its own rather than a
field on the role change. Readiness is a declaration ABOUT THE ROLE held — a Commando saying
"I am ready to command" is not what a Referee says — so a role change clears it. What the net
CALLS somebody does not change what they have agreed to do, and a rename that withdrew a
declaration would leave a Game Master hunting for one nobody retracted.

The response carries the whole roster, like the role change.

Requires staff access to the exercise — see the **games** tag for what that means — **or**
a game role holding `update` on `/games/participants` in this game. The game must be in `planning`
or `preparation`.

**CHANGING THE ROLE CLEARS READINESS**, and the clearing is the point rather than a side
effect. Readiness is a declaration ABOUT the role held: a Commando saying "I am ready to
command" is not the statement a Referee makes, and `is_judge_side` decides whether the gate
asks them at all. Keeping the flag across a role change would let somebody declare readiness
under one rule and have it counted under another — the cheapest possible way to start an
exercise whose only participant on the exercise side never confirmed anything.

**PROMOTING SOMEBODY TO THE JUDGE SIDE TAKES THEIR COMMAND AWAY.** A judge does not command, and
that rule is asked in BOTH directions: the unit, crew and hierarchy write paths refuse to GIVE a
command to a judge-side participant, and this route takes away what they already hold. Without
it the rule would hold only for commands granted after it was written — a Referee could keep
steering a hull simply by being made a Referee last.

- A HULL they commanded is **RELEASED**: it leaves the exercise, and its crew and map placement
  go with it. That is not a choice — `game_units.id_commander` is NOT NULL, so a hull cannot be
  left unsteerable, and there is nobody to move into the seat. What left is reported in
  `data.released_units`, by name, so the operator learns what the change cost.
- A TASK-ORGANISATION NODE they commanded merely LOSES ITS COMMANDER: the node stays, and so
  does everything under it. That is deliberately NOT reported, because nothing left the
  exercise — re-read `GET /games/{id}/hierarchy` to see it.

The response carries the whole roster, so the cleared `is_ready` is visible without a second
request.

**run this exercise** — the same rule as `POST /games/{id}/transitions`, and refused with 403
rather than 404 so a blocked pause stays visible in the audit trail.

The game must be in `execution`. **409 otherwise**, including at `closure`: a game under
analysis has no timeline running.

**A PAUSE IS A RATE, NOT A STATE.** It appends a segment of the rate series at factor zero and
closes the exercise to orders; the game stays in `execution`. There is no `paused` state, no
flag on the timeline, and **no catch-up on resume** — the paused wall-clock time is simply
never added to the assumed timeline, so a twenty-minute pause leaves the exercise twenty
minutes of scenario time behind where it would otherwise have been.

**TWO WRITES IN ONE TRANSACTION.** A clock stopped with the doors open accepts an order into a
frozen exercise; doors closed with the clock running means every hull keeps moving while
nobody can correct them. The segment is written first, so a failure to close the doors rolls
the stopped clock back with it.

**IDEMPOTENT IN EFFECT.** A second pause appends a second zero-rate segment, and zero either
side of zero is still zero. It does add a history row, because the history records what the
Game Master did and it did happen twice.

The response is the whole clock, so a client drawing a timeline needs no second call.

appends a segment, because "the rate was checked before a decisive phase" is something a

item.name: Where the fleet is at an assumed instant

query.description:
An instant on the **SCENARIO** clock, RFC 3339. Omitted, it means the scenario `now`,
computed by the server.

**THIS IS NOT THE WALL CLOCK.** Assumed time is a piecewise integral over the game's rate
changes, so it is routinely hours or days away from real time — a client that sent
`Date.now()` would be asking where the fleet was on a different day. This is also the
closure-playback parameter: pass an instant during the exercise and the answer is where every
hull was then, because each leg is a closed-form function of its own row.

The hull to measure every position FROM. When given, each position also carries
`distance_m`, `bearing_deg` and `relative_bearing_deg`.

**A MEASURE IS A QUERY, NOT A PROPERTY** — the README's §4 — because it depends on where
the question is asked from: the bearing from A to B is not the reciprocal of the bearing from
B to A, and the relative bearing depends on which way the observer happens to be pointing.
This is a parameter on one read rather than an endpoint of its own so that a range can never
contradict the plot it is displayed beside.

The hull must have a **position at this instant**; before the exercise begins none do, so any
value is refused. 400 naming the field rather than 404, because the parameter is not a path
segment and the hull may well be in the game.

**A HULL INSIDE ANOTHER THAT HAS NOT BEEN LET GO IS A 409, NAMING THE HULL HOLDING IT.** A
contained piece has no position of its own — it is absent from this read entirely, see below —
so it cannot be an observer, and the 400 above would send the operator looking for a hull that

request.description:
Authentication only, with **two ways in decided by the service**: the caller must be a
**participant of this game**, or hold `read` on `/system/games`. Like `GET /games/{id}`, and for
the same reason — Echo cannot express "this permission OR that participation" as a chain, and a
participant holds no application permission at all. Neither way in gives a **403**.

**A PARTICIPANT SEES THE WHOLE PLOT, INCLUDING THE OTHER SIDE AND THE JUDGES** (decided
2026-09-21). That is deliberately the **opposite** of `GET /games/{id}/units`, which stays
staff-facing so that a Commando does not learn the other side's order of battle — and the two
coexist because **the plot does not exist until the game begins**: positions come from the fix
chain, and the chain is empty until the transition into `execution` materialises an origin for
every placed hull. A participant who reads this during `planning` or `preparation` gets an empty
fleet at any instant they ask about, because no leg exists to answer with.

One state where a participant IS refused: **`closure`**, and for the same reason
`GET /games/{id}` refuses them there — the concept puts closure in the Game Master's and the
judges' hands. A judge-side participant, or the Game Master, still sees it.

**FOG OF WAR IS FUTURE WORK, deliberately not started.** When it arrives it belongs on this
decision rather than in a middleware, because it will be a per-hull visibility rule rather than
a yes/no.

**DERIVED POSITIONS, NOT MEASUREMENTS.** These come from the fix chain — where hulls were
ORDERED to be — and never from `unit_positions_latest`, which holds what a device reported. The
two are deliberately different tables: an order is clamped to the hull's specification and a
measurement is never clamped, so a vessel reporting 35 knots against a 30-knot specification is
the most interesting fact in the exercise rather than a bug to correct. The live feed is where
measured positions are read.

**EACH HULL IS ADVANCED ALONG ITS LEG**, not reported at the coordinates it was ordered from:
a hull two hours into a 12-knot leg is 24 nautical miles further on. A hull with no leg at or
before the instant is **absent** from the list — before the exercise begins that is every hull,
and the list is legitimately empty. The force itself is `GET /games/{id}/units`; this endpoint
deliberately does not enumerate hulls it cannot place, because a client would be tempted to
draw them at (0, 0), which is a real place in the Gulf of Guinea.

**THE THREE MEASURES APPEAR ONLY WHEN `from_unit` IS GIVEN**, and they are computed against the
observer's **live heading** — the heading of the leg in force at the instant asked about — so a
client holding a stale heading cannot get the wrong side of the ship. Bearing is a
**great-circle** bearing, not a rhumb one: §4 records that these are the measure queries, and
"which compass number do I point at" is the great-circle question.

**THE OBSERVER'S OWN ROW GETS A ZERO DISTANCE AND NO BEARING.** An azimuth between coincident
points does not exist, and `atan2(0, 0)` returns 0 — which would report a ship as bearing due
north of itself.

**A PIECE INSIDE ANOTHER IS NOT DRAWN** (decided 2026-10-06). A contained unit "takes no orders
of its own in the game until the host clears it": its position is its host's, and it is
**absent from this list** rather than drawn on top of the ship carrying it. The operator sees it
by drilling into the host's details, where `GET /games/{id}/units/{unit_id}/embarkations`
reports what is aboard and whether each piece has been let go.

**THE CLEARANCE IS WHAT PUTS IT BACK**, and it is the same line the order route and the
readiness gate draw: a piece its host has **let go** is its own contact, with a leg of its own —
the launch written at the host's position and heading — so it appears here like any other hull.
Being aboard is therefore not the rule; being aboard and **held** is. The exclusion reads the
**exercise's** composition and never the fleet register's, so a CMS edit cannot change what an
exercise draws.

**THE REALTIME PICTURE EXCLUDES IT TOO, BY CONSTRUCTION.** `game:<id>:positions` is built from
the same read this endpoint serves, and the protocol's rule is that an event carries exactly
what the corresponding read would have shown — so there is no second place for this rule to be
forgotten. See `docs/realtime-protocol.md`.

response.name:
Every hull that is its own contact and had a leg at or before the instant, ordered by hull.
A unit inside another is absent while its host holds it — see above.

item.name: Where a Telegram would come from, and who it may go to

query.description:
The node a **scenario role** speaks FROM. Required of the Game Master and the Judges and refused
of everybody else — see the description below.

request.description:
Requires `read` on `/games/messages` — the same permission as reading the traffic — and the game
must be in `execution`, on the same terms as sending one.

**THE CHAIN.** A Telegram is sent FROM a command post, and it may only be addressed to posts the
chain reaches. The chain between two posts is the path **up to their lowest common ancestor and
back down** — migration `000054`'s own words — and the posts strictly between are the
co-addressees (tembusan) the message MUST carry. Reaching past a post without copying it would
order somebody's force over their commander's head, which is what "skipping the chain" means.

**WHERE THE SENDER STANDS** decides the whole answer, and it is not the sender's to choose:

- a **commander** speaks from the post they hold. Naming `id_hierarchy_node` is a **400** —
  otherwise anybody could speak from the root and reach the whole force with no CC at all.
- the **Game Master and the Judges** speak as a scenario role (`[6.1]` requires it), and a scenario
  role is a name with no node behind it — "Panglima TNI" — so they MUST name `id_hierarchy_node`:
  the role says WHO, and the node says FROM WHERE.
- a participant who **commands nothing** has no place in the chain — **400**. The Game Master can
  give them a command, or send it for them.

**`blocked` IS RETURNED RATHER THAN DROPPED.** A post somebody commands that the chain cannot
reach is reported with the reason — a post with a force under it and nobody appointed to order it,
a hull nobody has placed, a force in another tree — because a recipient who is simply absent from
a list is indistinguishable from one who does not exist, and the operator's next action is always
to fix the thing named. A client that ignores `blocked` still gets a correct `addressees` list.

**THE SEND WALKS THE SAME TRAVERSAL.** `POST /games/{id}/messages` resolves the origin and the
chain through the same code this read uses, so a recipient offered here cannot be one the send
then refuses for another reason, and a copy this read says is required is the copy the send
demands. A picker built from anything else is a picker that can be wrong.

item.name: Record that the caller has read a message (A5)

request.description:
**A FUNCTIONAL RECEIPT, NOT A DISPLAY-ONLY ONE.** The client's answer to A5 was explicit that
the receipt matrix records **when each recipient read** the message, so this writes a real
timestamp that the sender can then see.

**`read_at` IS SET ONCE AND THE FIRST INSTANT IS KEPT.** The receipt answers "when did they
see it", and a receipt that followed the latest read would make a repeatedly-opened message
look like one nobody looked at for an hour. It also makes the write safe to repeat after a
dropped response.

**A BROADCAST HAS NO RECEIPT TO TAKE, AND THAT IS A 403 RATHER THAN A 404.** The message is
visible to the caller — that is why they could ask at all — so "not found" would be a lie; the
honest answer is that there is no row to mark, because a broadcast was addressed to nobody.

response.name: The message with the receipt recorded.

item.name: One message this caller may see

request.description:
**"NO SUCH MESSAGE" AND "NOT YOURS" ARE THE SAME ANSWER, ON PURPOSE.** Both are 404, because
telling a caller that a message exists but is not theirs is itself a disclosure — and for a
`RAHASIA` message it is the disclosure that matters.

**WHAT THE CALLER IS TOLD ABOUT THE SENDER DEPENDS ON WHO THEY ARE.** With an assumed identity
in play, `sender.assumed_role` is always present and `sender.author` is present only for the
Game Master, the Judges, and the sender themselves — Q13 hides the author from ordinary
participants and the answer to F5 reveals it to staff. When no identity was assumed there is
nothing to conceal, so `author` is present for everybody: the alternative would make the field
mean "the sender is not who they say" rather than "here is who really sent this", and a client
could not tell those apart.

response.name: The message, concealed as far as this caller is entitled.

item.name: Withdraw or hide a message — whichever the caller is entitled to

request.description:
**ONE ROUTE FOR BOTH OF A7'S DELETIONS, AND THE CALLER DOES NOT SAY WHICH.** The service infers
it, so a client cannot ask for the wrong one and cannot delete a message that is not theirs by
claiming the other verb.

| caller | effect |
|---|---|
| the sender | withdrawn from **every recipient**; still visible to the sender, the Game Master and the Judges, marked with when it went |
| an addressee | hidden from **that recipient alone**; the sender still sees it and is told they deleted it |
| anybody else | **403** — a broadcast is visible to everyone and addressed to nobody, so there is no row to write |

**NOTHING IS EVER HARD-DELETED.** A7 keeps the record for the Game Master and the Judges, and
closure playback must render the visibility as it was **at that instant** — otherwise a Judge
sees a message the personnel provably could not have seen.

**A SENDER WHO ALSO ADDRESSED THEMSELVES GETS THE SENDER'S DELETION.** The tie is broken that
way because the sender's act affects other people and is therefore the one they mean; breaking
it the other way would silently make the button do nothing to anybody else.

**IDEMPOTENT, AND THE FIRST INSTANT IS KEPT.** A second deletion succeeds without moving the
timestamp, so the record answers "when did they withdraw it" rather than "when was this
endpoint last called".

response.name:
The message after the deletion, carrying the timestamp that was written. A sender sees
`sender_deleted_at`; an addressee sees their own entry in `recipients` marked `deleted`.

clock is paused: several messages then share one assumed instant, and ordering by it would
shuffle messages whose real order the participants remember.

request.description:
**SENDING IS A PARTICIPANT'S ACT, NOT A STAFF ONE.** A Commando sends Telegram messages — [6]
has them passing "between Personnels or Actor" — so this asks for a place in the game and the
`send_message` permission, not for the ability to run the exercise.

**THE PHASE IS `execution`.** A message sent in `planning` has no scenario instant to sit on,
and one sent in `closure` would have to be placed on a timeline nobody is advancing.

**`[6.1]` IS ENFORCED, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.** A Telegram message from the Game Master or a
Judge **must** name `id_assumed_role`: the concept says that staff who want to send one "are
required to 'Act' as some kind of a Commando", so a staff Telegram without one is the Game
Master speaking as themselves into a channel the concept says they do not speak in. The
converse is refused too — a **participant may not assume an identity**, because allowing it
would make the concealment voluntary and anybody could send as anybody.

**`[6.2]` IS ENFORCED IN THE SERVICE.** Administrative messages are "used between Judges and
Game Master", so a participant on the exercise side sending `kind: administrative` is refused
with 403 naming `kind`. It is checked there rather than by a permission because the permission
cannot see the kind, and a permission per kind would put a grant in the matrix that the route
then refuses.

**A PERSONA ALSO NAMES WHERE IT SPEAKS FROM.** A scenario role is a name with no place behind
it — "Panglima TNI" says who is speaking and nothing about where — so a staff Telegram needs
`id_hierarchy_node` as well as `id_assumed_role`. It is the same pair that
`GET /games/{id}/messages/addressing` takes, so the recipient list a client builds from that
read is the list this send is judged against. A **participant** may not name a node: a commander
speaks from the post they hold, and a sender who could choose their own node could speak from
the task organisation's root and reach the whole force with no copies at all.

**A TELEGRAM TRAVELS THE CHAIN, SO ITS ADDRESSES ARE CHECKED AGAINST THE TASK ORGANISATION.**
The chain is the path from the sender up to the lowest common ancestor and back down, and every
post in the middle is a commander the message must be **copied** to. Sending from one hull to
another under the same node therefore requires that node's commander in `cc`. A recipient who
commands **no post** is refused, because a chain runs between *posts* and there is none to them;
so is a recipient the chain cannot reach, with the reason named. **Extra copies are allowed** —
`[7.12.3]`'s CC means "keep this commander informed", so copying somebody the chain does not
require tells more people rather than fewer, and refusing it would be this API's rule and not
the concept's.

**THE CHAIN APPLIES TO TELEGRAMS ONLY.** An administrative message passes between the Game
Master and the Judges as a conversation, so it has no chain to walk and nobody to copy; applying
the rule to it would refuse the one exchange `[6.2]` allows to be unaddressed. So
`id_hierarchy_node` is **unused** on an administrative message rather than refused on one —
nothing about a message's origin is stored for either kind, which makes that field validation
input rather than a record.

**AN UNADDRESSED MESSAGE IS A BROADCAST (A2), AND ONLY `TERBUKA` MAY BE ONE.** Omitting both
`to` and `cc` makes the message visible to every participant; naming a recipient for a
`TERBATAS` or `RAHASIA` message is required, because A1 gates those two on the recipient list
and an unaddressed one would mean different things to its sender and to everybody else.

**ONE PERSON IS ONE ROW.** A user in both `to` and `cc` is refused rather than silently
collapsed: the two lists mean different things — [7.12.2] addresses, [7.12.3] copies — and a
collapse would lose which one the sender meant while looking like success.

item.name: Record a judgement about a participant's action

request.description:
**CONCEPT `[1.6]`: "Game Master and Judges are able to give Judgement for every actions that are
taken by each Personnels. (Turning the Bearings, Adjusting the Speed, Route Taken, etc)".**

**APPEND-ONLY.** There is no update route and no delete route, and neither is an omission to be
filled in later: a score that can be quietly rewritten is not evidence, and the point of the
record is that the Judges' assessment of an exercise survives it. A corrected score is a new
judgement.

**THE JUDGE IS THE CALLER, AND IS NEVER NAMED IN THE BODY.** A request that could name one
would let a Judge file a mark under somebody else's name. The caller must hold `judge` on
`/games/judgements` and be a participant of this exercise.

**`score` IS FREE TEXT.** The client answered this directly (Q6): a judge types `85`, `Baik`, or
a sentence. The name reads numeric because `[1.6]` says "Points", but the client has never
supplied a scale — a numeric field would invent one and then reject the strings their judges
actually write.

**`id_fix` IS OPTIONAL AND SHOULD USUALLY BE OMITTED.** A judgement about one order cites the
leg from the fix chain that recorded it; a judgement about a person's conduct cites nothing.
Forcing a leg would make the operator pick one arbitrarily, and an arbitrary citation is
indistinguishable from a real one.

| field | refused when | status |
|---|---|---|
| `id_personnel` | the person is not in this exercise | 400 |
| `id_fix` | the action is not a recorded order of this exercise | 400 |
| `id_personnel` | it names the caller — nobody marks their own work | 400 |
| `score` | it is blank or only whitespace | 400 |
| — | the scenario clock has not started | 409 |

variable.description: The scenario's id, scoped to the game.
The step's id, scoped to its scenario.

request.description:
**A SUB-STEP IS ONE COMMAND TO ONE AUDIENCE**, which is what a step used to be. Adding one here gives
the step a second audience: the paragraph that used to say "TF Alpha attacks north while KRI Charlie
holds station" becomes two commands that each commander can read without the other's.

**THE ANSWER IS THE WHOLE SCENARIO**, on the same terms every step write answers with it: a command's
meaning is its position among its siblings, so a client that added one needs the list that orders it
rather than the row it touched.

**A `beat` HAS NO SUB-STEPS**, and adding one to it is `409` — the kind says the step obliges nobody,
and a command without an audience contradicts it. The refusal names the remedy: send `kind: orders` if
the step really carries commands.

**THE AUDIENCE IS A SECOND WRITE.** A new command reaches nobody until
`PUT .../substeps/{substep_id}/related` names who it is for, which is how the editor's two panes work:
the text is typed in one and the units picked in the other.

request.description:
**THE ANSWER IS THE RESOLUTION, NOT THE STORED REFS**: what the step names, and who must declare
ready because of it.

**THE LIST IS DERIVED — the union of the step's SUB-STEPS' lists, deduped.** A step no longer carries a
related list of its own: since 000097 the list belongs to a sub-step, because a sub-step is one command
to one audience. Two commands naming the same task group is normal, and the audience is the set of
posts they name — which is what the readiness gate counts.

**THE RULE IS THE SPINE'S.** A related **hull** brings its commander and nobody else aboard; a
related **node** brings its own commander *and* the commander of every hull beneath it, however
deep. `models.Addressing.RelatedPersonnel` decides that, and it is the same traversal the message
chain walks — so the rule a readiness gate refuses somebody with cannot drift from the rule a
message is addressed by. A post nobody commands brings nobody rather than failing: a node with no
commander still resolves the hulls under it.

**A PERSON REACHED TWICE APPEARS ONCE**, attributed to the first ref that named them, so the list
is a function of the step rather than of the order the traversal ran in.

**THIS IS READ IN EVERY STATE, INCLUDING `closure`.** A Game Master reviewing a finished exercise
needs to see who the plan obliged, and the readiness gate reads this same answer while the exercise
runs — only the write closes with the book.

request.description:
**THIS ROUTE ALWAYS ANSWERS 409.** A step no longer carries a related list, because the list is the
audience of ONE command and a command is a sub-step. The sentence names the route that works:
`PUT /games/{id}/scenarios/{scenario_id}/steps/{step_id}/substeps/{substep_id}/related`.

**THE ROUTE IS KEPT RATHER THAN REMOVED** so a client that has not been updated is told why. Accepting
the body as a shortcut — writing the same list onto every sub-step — would be a second way to say one
thing, and the first time the two disagreed a readiness gate would wait for people nobody had
addressed. Ignoring it would be worse still: the client would believe an audience had been recorded.

item.name: Whether a step may start, and who is holding it back

variable.description: The scenario's id, scoped to the game.
The step's id, scoped to its scenario — a sibling's step is 404, like every other step route.

request.description:
**THE GATE IS THE GAME-LEVEL ONE AT STEP GRANULARITY.** `GameReadiness` asks whether an EXERCISE
may leave preparation — a window, a force, placed, with somebody commanding it, and everybody on the
exercise side ready. This asks whether a STEP may start, and its condition is about people only:
the personnel §6.2's related list resolves to, and whether they have declared.

**WHO IS ASKED IS NOT WHO IS RESOLVED.** A participant who judges is named by the resolution and is
**never waited for** — concept [2.3] takes the Judges out of the declaration — and a hull's
commander is a column on the piece that nothing constrains to the roster, so somebody who is not in
the exercise can be named too. Both are counted in `excluded`, and each person carries `asked`, so a
screen can grey a referee out rather than showing them as not ready. Counting either would leave a
step unstartable for ever.

**TWO EMPTY SHAPES ARE REFUSED RATHER THAN PASSED.** "Everybody has declared" is *true* of a step
that names nobody, so a gate written as `ready == required` would wave an unfinished plan through;
the same hole repeats when the posts a step names oblige nobody at all (a node with no commander and
no hulls beneath it, or commanders who judge). Each refusal names a different remedy in `reason`.

**`reason` IS PRESENT ONLY WHEN THE STEP MAY NOT START**, and it is the sentence the gate itself
refuses with — a build that explained one rule on screen and refused with another would be two
rules.

**THE READ IS OPEN IN EVERY STATE, INCLUDING `closure`.** Nothing starts a step before execution and
nothing starts one after closure, but a Game Master reviewing a finished exercise is asking exactly
who was supposed to be ready — the same asymmetry the book's own reads have.
**WHAT IT COUNTS IS A DECLARATION FOR THIS STEP IN THIS ATTEMPT** (B48, closed 2026-10-07). Those
declarations live in a store of their own, keyed by the step AND the attempt, and are written by the
participant route on this same path (`PUT`/`DELETE`, below). A replay advances the attempt, so the
abandoned attempt's declarations stop being read and the step reads as outstanding again — without
anybody withdrawing anything, and without this read knowing that a replay happened.

**AND IT IS NOT A PARTICIPANT'S READ.** This route is gated on a game role holding `/games/scenarios`
`read` — the Game Master and the judge side. The people who must declare **cannot read the list they
are on**, and deliberately cannot read the plan at all: the script is precisely what the people being
exercised must not see. What they read instead is `GET /games/{id}/current-step`, which names the one
step being asked of them and nothing else.

request.description:
**THE PARTICIPANT'S OWN WRITE, AND THE ROUTE A STEP'S GATE WAITS FOR.** The gate is asked when the Game
Master presses `Play`, so a declaration has to be made BEFORE a step starts — and because a replay
advances the attempt, the abandoned attempt's declarations stop counting and the same people declare
again through this same call, with nothing else to do in between.

**THE STEP DOES NOT HAVE TO BE PLAYING, AND USUALLY IS NOT.** Declaring while nothing is playing is the
ordinary case: it is the only moment at which a replay's fresh gate can be satisfied. The exercise only
has to be in `execution`, because a declaration is a fact about a step that is being played.

**THE STEP MUST ASK THE CALLER.** A step's related list resolves to the people it obliges, and only
those may declare — a participant the step does not concern is refused **403**, and the judge side is
refused **409** rather than accepted-and-ignored, because a referee's declaration counts towards nothing
and a `200` would tell them it did.

**A STEP THE EXERCISE HAS ALREADY REACHED IS REFUSED (409).** The gate it belongs to has been asked, so
a declaration cannot count towards anything; the refusal says so and names the remedy, which is that a
replay asks again. A client holding a stale Ready button is exactly what this is for.

**PRESSING IT TWICE IS ONE DECLARATION WITH A LATER INSTANT**, not an error: the same present fact,
stated again.

**THE REMEDY FOR THE ONE MISTAKE THE ROUTE ABOVE INVITES** — a commander who pressed Ready and then
found they were not. It is the caller's OWN declaration and nobody else's: there is no way here to
withdraw somebody else's readiness.

reached is refused too, because the gate it belongs to has been asked, and a change to a declaration
that can no longer count is a change to nothing.

request.description:
**THIS IS WHERE THE READINESS GATE BITES.** The step's related personnel must all have declared — the
same list, resolved the same way, that `GET .../readiness` reports — and a step whose people are not
ready is refused **409 with that read's own sentence**, so a client that explained why the button was
disabled sees the identical words when the request is refused anyway.

**TWO MORE REFUSALS, EACH WITH ITS OWN REMEDY:** the exercise is not in `execution` (409, naming the
state — a book is written before the exercise runs and a step is played while it runs), and the
exercise is **already on a step** (409). The last one comes from the database: a partial unique index
allows one playing step per exercise, which is the only version of "one step at a time" that two
concurrent callers cannot both pass.

**NOTHING IS SENT.** The instant the run is stamped with comes from the exercise's own clock, for the
reason the order and drag routes give: a client that stamped its own could put a step anywhere in the
timeline. The answer is the run itself, so a client needs no second call to draw the panel.

**IN A `scenario` EXERCISE THIS ALSO STARTS THE CLOCK**, and that is what makes a beat the thing
the exercise moves inside. A scenario exercise enters `execution` with a rate of zero and runs
only while a step is playing, so `Play` is the only thing that starts it — a `maneuver` or
`static` exercise is untouched, because nothing plays beats in either. A Game Master may still
pause, resume and re-rate the clock INSIDE the beat on the ordinary clock routes.

response.name: The step is playing.

item.name: Move past a step without playing it

variable.description: The scenario's id, scoped to the game.
The step's id, scoped to its scenario.

request.description:
**THE GATE DOES NOT APPLY, AND THE OVERRIDE IS RECORDED** (client, 2026-10-01). A skip is the Game
Master saying "we are not waiting for this one", so a step with people outstanding may be skipped —
and the answer says **how many were still waiting** (`outstanding_at_start`) with
`overrode_readiness` true. The pair is held in step by the database, so a skip past three people
cannot be recorded as if it were routine.

**THE CLOCK JUMPS PAST THE STEP'S WINDOW**, as a segment with source `skip` carrying a signed
assumed-time delta — the same primitive a rewind uses, in the other direction — and the rate carries
through unchanged: a skip moves the clock, it does not change how fast it runs. Two cases jump
**nothing** and are not errors: a step with no window (there is no end to reach), and a window
already behind the clock (jumping backwards would be a rewind, which is a different control).

**THE SEGMENT AND THE RECORD COMMIT TOGETHER**, or neither does: a skip that moved the clock without
recording why leaves a hole in the history, and one that recorded the skip without moving leaves the
exercise waiting on a step the Game Master abandoned.

**IN A `scenario` EXERCISE THE JUMP LANDS ON A RATE OF ZERO** — a skip ENDS a beat, and no beat
is playing afterwards. A `maneuver` exercise keeps the behaviour this jump was written for: the
segment repeats the rate in force, moving the clock without changing how fast it runs.

response.name: The step was skipped, and the clock moved past it.

item.name: End the step the exercise is on

variable.description: The scenario's id, scoped to the game.

The step's id — and it must be the step the exercise is ON, because a route nested under a step that
ended a different one would not be doing what it says.

request.description:
**THE CONTROL THAT MAKES A SEQUENCE POSSIBLE.** Play and skip both refuse while a step is playing, so
without this an exercise could play its first step and then only be refused. Ending **frees the
partial unique index** — the row stops being `playing` — which is what lets the next step start.

**IT MOVES THE CLOCK TO THE END OF THE BEAT'S WINDOW.** Ending a beat gives it its FULL WINDOW: when
the step's window end is still ahead of the exercise's clock, the clock is advanced to it — the same
rule an order follows when its step's window has not opened yet — so ending a step early does not leave
the exercise behind its plan, and the next beat starts from where the plan says this one finished. A
window already behind the clock, or a step with no window at all, contributes no jump: this never moves
time backwards. A `skip` reaches the same end-of-window instant, so the two controls are told apart by
what they do with the orders rather than by where they leave the clock.

**BETWEEN STEPS IS A REAL STATE**, which is why the end is explicit rather than implied by the next
play: a scenario's steps are beats, and the time between them is the exercise — the fleet keeps
steering and orders keep arriving. What finishes with the beat is the clock (below); what does not is
the exercise's readiness to take orders.

**THE STEP IN THE PATH MUST BE THE ONE PLAYING**, or 409 saying so. Calling it when nothing is playing
is also 409 — an exercise between steps is a state, not an error to be tolerated.

**AND IN A `scenario` EXERCISE IT STOPS THE CLOCK AND LANDS IT ON THE WINDOW'S END**, in ONE segment:
a rate of zero and the forward jump together, sourced `end`. That is what makes the exercise stop moving
between its beats, since every position in the system is derived from the assumed clock. It deliberately
does **not** close the exercise to orders: those stay open, because the orders a Commander gives
between beats are the ones the next `Play` releases.

**AND IT HANDS NOTHING ON.** A skip releases the orders the beat was holding and records how many
people were still outstanding; an end leaves the orders waiting for the next beat and records no
override, because ending a step is not abandoning it. Those two are what separate the controls.

response.name: The run as it now stands — a `played` step with its end instant.

item.name: Replay a step — rewind to its start and erase the abandoned attempt

variable.description: The scenario's id, scoped to the game.
The step to replay — the exercise goes back to where THIS step began.

request.description:
**THE OPERATION THE ATTEMPT AND THE ERASURE WERE BUILT FOR.** The exercise's clock goes back to the
instant the step STARTED, and everything the abandoned attempt did from that instant onward is
**erased**: the orders and the drags, the device reports, the telegrams, the movement modes the hulls
were switched into, and any judgement that cited one of those actions (client, 2026-10-01 —
`docs/client-questions.md` ROUND 7). Closure then replays the CLEAN run.

**A REAL ERASURE, THOUGH A SOFT ONE.** Every erased row survives in the database with `deleted_by`
naming the account that asked, and every read filters it out — so the fix chain, which is the POSITION
record, is never unrecoverably destroyed. The erasure is bounded by the SPAN rather than by the
attempt: rows written BEFORE the step started belong to the clean run and are kept.

**REPLAYING IS ALSO GOING BACK AND FORTH ON THE ASSUMED CLOCK.** The response says where play
resumes (the step's own start, as the run recorded it) and the exercises's `epoch` advances, so the
replay's own orders cannot be mistaken for the ones it disowned.

**THE POSITIONS DO NOT NEED RESTORING.** They come back from the fix chain itself — the rows from
before the rewind point survive and are answered exactly as they were — and each hull keeps steaming
along the leg that was already in force. A hull's MOVEMENT MODE is the one thing that cannot be
derived, because it is a column holding current state, and it is put back from the snapshot taken when
the step was played.

**THE FRESH GATE, AND NOTHING IS WITHDRAWN TO MAKE IT FRESH.** This advances the exercise's `epoch`,
and a step's declarations belong to an attempt (B48, closed 2026-10-07) — so the declarations of the
attempt being abandoned simply stop being read, and the people the step obliges must declare once
more. There is no flag to re-arm and nothing to undo: the advance IS the reset. The route that
re-declares is `PUT /games/{id}/scenarios/{scenario_id}/steps/{step_id}/readiness`, which a client
reaches from `GET /games/{id}/current-step`.

**409** when the exercise is not in `execution`, and **409** when the step has not been reached yet —
a replay goes back to where a step BEGAN, and a step that never began has no such instant.

response.name: What the replay cost and what it changed.

item.name: Append a step to a scenario

variable.description: The scenario's id, scoped to the game.

request.description:
**`content` MAY BE EMPTY.** A plan is authored while it is being written, so a step whose text is
still to come is a legitimate state rather than a broken row.

**THE WINDOW IS OPTIONAL AND IS A PAIR.** Both `start_hour` and `end_hour` or neither: one end
without the other is 400, because a half-window is a state the schema cannot hold and filling the
missing end in from the next step would invent a time the author never chose.

**`HHMM` IS STRICT** — four digits, `0900` and not `900`, no separator, `2400` refused (the day ends
at `2359`) — and the end must be AFTER the start. A window does not cross midnight: `2330`–`0030` is
refused, and an exercise that needs one expresses it as two steps.

**THE STEP ORDER AND THE WINDOWS MUST AGREE.** A new step goes last, so a window that begins before
the previous step's window ENDED is refused with 400: the book would otherwise describe an exercise
that walks backwards through its own timeline. Steps with no window impose nothing and are skipped.

response.name: The scenario, with the new step in its place.

item.name: Add a scenario to the end of the book

request.description:
**ALWAYS APPENDED.** A new scenario goes last, because that is what a caller asks for by not saying
where; a caller that wants it elsewhere sends the order it wants to `PUT /games/{id}/scenarios/order`
— the same write the authoring UI makes for a drag.

**THIS IS HOW A DETACHED MISSION IS USED FOR A GAME.** Send `id_mission` and the template's title,
description, steps and related hulls become this exercise's plan: each related hull is mapped to the
game's existing piece, or enrolled into the force when the exercise does not hold it. Send `code` (or
nothing) instead to author a plan from scratch under a new Kode Misi.

**SCENARIO EXERCISES ONLY** (409). A `maneuver` or `static` exercise is simulated from orders or
positioned by hand and has no beats, so it cannot hold a plan; the sentence names the mode, and a GM
may correct it with `PATCH /games/{id}` while the exercise is still in `planning`. Reads are
deliberately NOT gated — a game whose mode was corrected keeps its plan readable at closure.

**REFUSED UNLESS THE EXERCISE IS IN `planning` OR `preparation`** (409), and refused to a caller who
is not a participant of THIS exercise (403): the route's gate also admits an application
administrator, which is right for reading any exercise and wrong for authoring one.

**A GAME HOLDS EXACTLY ONE SCENARIO**, so this is also refused with 409 when one already exists; delete
it first to attach a different mission.

**TWO ADDS AT ONCE COME BACK AS 409**, because both read the same last position and one of them
loses at the unique index. The same request succeeds unchanged, which is what the status means.

request.description:
**THE AUTHOR RULE IS THE WHOLE OF THIS ROUTE.** Only the person who filed a review may change
it, and the caller IS the author — no request field can name one. The refusal for somebody
else's review is **403 and not 404**, which is worth stating because the conventional choice for
an authorization rule is the opposite: a 404 normally declines to confirm that a row exists.
That reasoning does not apply here, because the caller is staff who can already READ every
review in this exercise through the list. There is nothing left to conceal, so the specific
answer costs nothing and tells a client with a stale control what actually went wrong.

**ONLY `body` CHANGES.** `id_personnel` is deliberately absent: moving a review from one person
to another is not a revision of what was written, it is a different review, and allowing it
would let an author retarget a note after seeing how it read.

**THIS IS THE ONE ROUTE IN THIS API WHOSE AUTHORITY DEPENDS ON THE ROW RATHER THAN THE ROLE**,
and it is the deliberate asymmetry with `/games/judgements`, which has no update route at all. A
judgement is evidence about an action, and a score that can be quietly rewritten is not
evidence; a review is the analyst's conclusion, and sharpening your own conclusion is the work.

`revised` becomes `true` and `updated_at` moves. `created_at` does not, so the record of when
the observation was first made survives the edit.

response.name: The review as it stands after the edit.

item.name: Closure's replay — every action taken, on the scenario clock

query.description:
Earliest scenario instant, inclusive, as RFC 3339 — for example
`2026-09-22T13:00:00+07:00`. Omitted means the exercise's beginning.

This is an **assumed**-clock instant and not a real one, which is why a clock event's own
stored instant never appears here: the window is compared against the derived instant.
Latest scenario instant, inclusive. Omitted means the exercise's end.

Narrows to one stream. **The six ranks are the sort order**, so `transition` events sort
before `step`, `step` before `clock`, `clock` before `order`, `order` before `message`, and
`message` before `judgement` when they share an instant.

`transition` is a phase move — `planning -> preparation`, `preparation -> execution`,
`execution -> closure` — and it is FIRST because a phase change is a precondition for
everything that follows it. It is also the sharpest case of the rule: the move into
`execution` happens in the same transaction that anchors the clock, so it shares its instant
with the exercise's opening clock event exactly.

`step` is a step of the scenario book being played or skipped, and it is SECOND for that same
reason one level down: **a skip writes the run and the clock jump together**, so they can land
on the same instant, and the step is the decision while the jump is its consequence. They do
not ALWAYS share one — with the clock running they sit a fraction of a second apart — and the
rank is what settles it when they do.

**A move appears here only once the game is anchored.** A start declared in Planning anchors
it from the beginning and its early moves land on the scenario origin; a game whose start was
never declared has no scenario instant before Execution, so those moves are absent.

Narrows to the events attributable to one person: **the orders they gave, the messages they
sent, and the judgements about them**. That asymmetry is deliberate — a judgement is written
about a person rather than by one, and the read a debrief is built from wants the marks
against somebody, not the ones they awarded.

Narrows to the **orders for one hull**, and it is the one filter that EXCLUDES the other
streams rather than narrowing them: only an order belongs to a hull. A message is addressed
to people and a judgement is about a person, so neither is returned under this filter.

Continues from where the previous page ended. **Opaque — pass back the `next_cursor` you were
given rather than constructing one.** A cursor carries the whole sort tuple, so a
hand-built one that named only an instant would resume in the middle of a group of events
sharing that instant, which on a paused exercise is every event there is.

Page size. Optional with a default of **100**, which is larger than every other list here
because a client-side playback wants a window in memory rather than a page. Capped at 200.

request.description:
**CONCEPT §4: "Closure is where the 'Game Master' and 'Judges' analyze the 'Game Play'. In this
phase they can view each action taken by each Personnels with playback-like feature (slider or
some sort)."** And §4 answers *who*: *"The closure phase is only accessible by the 'Game Master'
and 'Judges'"*. So a caller must hold `read` on `/games/timeline` **and** be a participant of this
exercise.

**A MERGE OF FOUR STREAMS IN ONE SEQUENCE ON THE SCENARIO CLOCK.** Orders, messages, judgements
and changes to the clock itself, ordered by `assumed_at` and then by a **pinned tiebreak**:
events share an instant routinely — several orders arrive in one tick, and **during a pause the
clock does not move at all, so every action taken while paused carries the identical instant** —
so the sort is on `(assumed_at, type rank, id)` and all three are part of the cursor. Two
identical requests cannot return one instant's events in two different orders.

**THE `order` STREAM CARRIES ORDERS, DRAGS *AND* DEPARTURES**, and `data.kind` is what tells them
apart. A `leg` is a heading and a speed a Commando gave; a `jump` (A11) is a position somebody
**set** by hand in a `static` exercise, which is why its `heading_deg` and `speed_kn` are both zero
and its `was_clamped` is false — there is no order in it to clamp; a `launch` is a **departure**, a
unit leaving its host under way, carrying the host's heading and the host's speed. The entry's
`type` stays `order` because it names the STREAM rather than the act, the way every other source
names where an entry came from; so a client drawing a course line must switch on `data.kind` first,
or it will draw a drag as a hull holding due north at nought knots.

**A DEPARTURE IS THE ONE ROW THAT NAMES TWO HULLS** (2026-10-06). `data.id_host`, `data.host_name`
and `data.host_hull_number` are present on it and `null` on everything else, and `ordered_by` is
then whoever **let the unit go** rather than whoever ordered a movement — which is the honest
reading of "the person responsible for this entry", and the same reading a drag gets for the person
who dragged it. **It is the only record of that fact anywhere**: a detach deletes the embarkation
row, so a replay cannot learn from the composition that the piece was ever aboard. In a `static`
exercise a departure is written as a `jump`, exactly as a drag is — so `id_host` is what
distinguishes them, and `kind` alone does not.

**NOTHING IS MASKED AND NOTHING IS FILTERED, AND THAT IS THE PHASE RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT.**
A8 makes withdrawn messages visible to the Game Master and the Judges, and F5 reveals identities
at Closure. So a withdrawn message IS returned, carrying `sender_deleted_at` **and** each
recipient's `deleted_at`; and a message sent under an assumed identity carries the assumed role
**and** the real author, because the concealment is part of what is being analysed rather than
something to be tidied away.

**A CLOCK EVENT'S `assumed_at` IS COMPUTED, AND THE RESULT IS WORTH KNOWING.** The stored instant
is on the REAL clock, so the scenario instant is derived from it. Two consequences a client will
see: the opening event lands exactly on the instant the exercise's scenario clock started, and a
pause and the resume that followed it can share one `assumed_at` — because from the scenario's
point of view no time passed between them.

**THE SEQUENCE IS STABLE, AND A CLIENT MAY RELY ON IT.** Closure is terminal: no orders arrive,
no messages are sent, no judgements are recorded. So a page taken now is the same page taken
later, and the whole replay can be held for the life of the phase. That is what makes the
analysis meaningful, and it is a property of the lifecycle rather than a promise this endpoint
invents.

query.description:
Earliest scenario instant, inclusive, as RFC 3339 — for example
`2026-09-22T13:00:00+07:00`. Omitted means the exercise's beginning.

This is an **assumed**-clock instant and not a real one, which is why a clock event's own
stored instant never appears here: the window is compared against the derived instant.
Latest scenario instant, inclusive. Omitted means the exercise's end.

Narrows to one stream. **The six ranks are the sort order**, so `transition` events sort
before `step`, `step` before `clock`, `clock` before `order`, `order` before `message`, and
`message` before `judgement` when they share an instant.

`transition` is a phase move — `planning -> preparation`, `preparation -> execution`,
`execution -> closure` — and it is FIRST because a phase change is a precondition for
everything that follows it. It is also the sharpest case of the rule: the move into
`execution` happens in the same transaction that anchors the clock, so it shares its instant
with the exercise's opening clock event exactly.

`step` is a step of the scenario book being played or skipped, and it is SECOND for that same
reason one level down: **a skip writes the run and the clock jump together**, so they can land
on the same instant, and the step is the decision while the jump is its consequence. They do
not ALWAYS share one — with the clock running they sit a fraction of a second apart — and the
rank is what settles it when they do.

**A move appears here only once the game is anchored.** A start declared in Planning anchors
it from the beginning and its early moves land on the scenario origin; a game whose start was
never declared has no scenario instant before Execution, so those moves are absent.

Narrows to the events attributable to one person: **the orders they gave, the messages they
sent, and the judgements about them**. That asymmetry is deliberate — a judgement is written
about a person rather than by one, and the read a debrief is built from wants the marks
against somebody, not the ones they awarded.

Narrows to the **orders for one hull**, and it is the one filter that EXCLUDES the other
streams rather than narrowing them: only an order belongs to a hull. A message is addressed
to people and a judgement is about a person, so neither is returned under this filter.

Continues from where the previous page ended. **Opaque — pass back the `next_cursor` you were
given rather than constructing one.** A cursor carries the whole sort tuple, so a
hand-built one that named only an instant would resume in the middle of a group of events
sharing that instant, which on a paused exercise is every event there is.

because a client-side playback wants a window in memory rather than a page. Capped at 200.

item.name: Author an identity for staff to send under

request.description:
**CONCEPT `[1.12]`: "Game Master can create Scenario Role (eg. Panglima TNI). This can be used
to send Telegram Message while in Execution Phase".** They are **per game** and belong to it —
the same peacetime name may be issued by two exercises without either knowing about the other —
which is why they hang off the game rather than living with the application's role vocabulary.

**STAFF ONLY.** A participant creating one would be minting a name to impersonate with, and the
concealment Q13 exists to provide would become voluntary.

**THIS IS WHAT MAKES A STAFF TELEGRAM POSSIBLE.** [6.1] requires the Game Master and the Judges
to act as somebody, so a game with no scenario roles cannot produce a Telegram message from
staff at all — the send is refused with 400 naming `id_assumed_role` until one exists.

request.description:
**Reached by authentication alone — no application permission.** Two kinds of caller arrive
here, and the service decides between them IN THIS ORDER:

1. a **participant** — anyone holding a place in this game. They see it through the rules
   below, which means `area` and `map_tag` are withheld until the exercise starts.
2. **staff** — a caller holding `read` on `/system/games`, who sees all of it. An operator
   reviewing a plan is not a participant, and withholding the area from them during
   Preparation would withhold it precisely when the Game Master is placing units against it.

A caller who is neither is refused with **403** — not 404, because the game plainly exists
and they may have seen it in a list a moment ago.

The participant check runs FIRST, and the order is a security decision rather than a
preference: an administrator who is also playing a Commando is treated as the participant
they are, so the area stays withheld during Preparation and the game is refused at Closure.

The response depends on WHO is asking and WHICH state the game is in. Two fields are
withheld from participants rather than being absent from the schema:

* `area` and `map_tag` are returned to the Game Master and Judges at every state, and to
  Commandos and unit personnel only from `execution` onward. The concept is explicit:
  personnel "does not know where the 'Game Area' is until it is Executed".

They are OMITTED, not nulled, which is why both are optional in the schema. A participant
during Preparation still needs the name and state to render "waiting for readiness", so
refusing the whole resource would deny them information they are entitled to.

In `closure` this endpoint is refused to participants entirely — 403. That is a different
mechanism from withholding: the concept ejects personnel from Closure, so there is
nothing in that state they may see.

There is no mode-conditional exception here any more. The note that used to sit at this
point concerned Operational, where withholding the area bought nothing because a Commando
was physically inside it — and Operational is no longer a game mode at all. The rule now
applies to every game there is, so it needs no exception.

response.name: The game, as this caller may see it.

`planning`.

A soft delete, and it exists for exactly one situation: a game created in error. Once a
game has been prepared or run it is a record of an exercise, and the concept asks for
game HISTORY — so it is retired, not erased. 409 while the game is past `planning`.

Because Planning is where everything else is attached, a game can only be discarded while
nothing depends on it. That is the same rule the unit taxonomy uses when it refuses to
retire a class that still holds live hulls, for the same reason: a cascade here would be
invisible in the audit trail.

item.name: Enter a game room with its key

request.description:
The room key is the ONLY input: the client does not know the game id yet, which is exactly
what this call is for. It answers with the game AND the caller's own participant row, so a
freshly installed app learns in one request what it has entered, what it may do there, and
whether it has already declared readiness.

**Authentication only.** What authorises the call is holding a place in the game the key
belongs to — an instance fact, which a Casbin object cannot express because objects name
resource families and carry no instance id.

**A wrong key is 404** — the same 404 a discarded game produces, so the endpoint cannot be
used to tell a key that never existed from one whose exercise was cancelled.

**A valid key held by a non-participant is 403.** Not 404: they hold a real key, so the room
plainly exists, and telling them otherwise would send them hunting for a typo in a key that
is correct. The remedy is to ask the Game Master for a place, and only a 403 says that. It
leaks nothing — a guessed key is never the valid one, so somebody guessing only ever sees
the 404.

**Refused at `closure`** for a participant the rules eject from it, on the same terms as
`GET /games/{id}`. Both refusals exist because one is not enough: a participant who cannot
READ a game must not be able to enter it through the other door either.

The key is stored unhashed, unlike every other secret in this API, because it is
TRANSCRIBED — read aloud or copied off a board and typed into a handset — and a hash cannot
be read out. Migration 000017 records that as a decision rather than an oversight.

response.name: The game, and the caller's place in it.

request.description:
Accepts up to 60 fixes from one vessel's beacon. This is the endpoint the mobile app calls.

**Authorised by being this vessel's current commander — not by a permission.** A Casbin
object names a resource family and carries no instance id, so "may this user report for
THIS ship" is not expressible as a policy. The check is an instance comparison in the
service, and the same reasoning applies to `GET /live-feed/me`.

A refusal is **403, not 404**: the vessel exists and the caller may have listed it a moment
earlier, so reporting a blocked report as "not found" would hide it from the audit trail.
Only a vessel that genuinely does not exist is a 404.

## What the server does with `recorded_at`

The client sends when it *believes* it observed each fix; the server decides whether that
is a live report or a backlog.

| Gap from the server's clock | Treatment |
|---|---|
| within ±60 s | **live** — `recorded_at` is re-stamped with the server's time |
| older than 60 s, within 30 days | **backfill** — the device's `recorded_at` is kept |
| older than 30 days | **refused**, counted in `rejected` |

Re-stamping a live fix is not tidiness. A `recorded_at` in the future would become the
vessel's latest position, and the guard that discards out-of-order fixes would then discard
every honest fix until real time caught up — a ship reporting steadily that never moves on
the map. A device clock more than a minute ahead is therefore treated as live, re-stamped,
and logged as a warning.

Keeping a backfill's own timestamp is the mirror of the same argument: a backlog's whole
value is *where the vessel was when it could not report*, and re-stamping it to now would
draw a straight line the ship never sailed.

## Rejections

Age is the only per-fix refusal, and it is permanent — an out-of-retention fix cannot be
made valid by sending it again. The response therefore carries **counts**, not a list of
complaints with nothing to act on. A batch in which every fix was refused is still a
**200**: the request was understood and each fix was examined, and the counts are the
answer.

## Ordering

Fixes may arrive in any order, and the vessel's latest position is taken from the **newest
fix in the batch by `recorded_at`** — not the last one sent. A backlog flushed after a
reconnect interleaves old points among new ones, so the last one sent is frequently not the
newest one observed.

response.name:
How the batch was handled. Every response to a well-formed batch is 200, including one
in which nothing was accepted.

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/live-feed`.

Every live vessel and its last known position. This is what the desktop command centre
renders.

**Vessels that have never reported are included, with no `position` key.** A map that omits

**Not paginated, deliberately.** A page of a standing picture is an incomplete picture, and
an incomplete map is a wrong one. The set is bounded by the navy's vessel count, and every
caller who may read it may read all of it.

so ages within a single reply are comparable with each other.

item.name: Add a level to the unit hierarchy

request.description:
Requires `create` on `/system/hierarchy`.

**THE INTERESTING CASE IS INSERTING IN THE MIDDLE.** A future Koarmada belongs between Gugus
and Operasi Gabungan, and a level below Unsur is the same problem at the other end, so the
request says WHERE the new level goes rather than what number it gets. The server renumbers.

`insert_after_id` names the level the new one ranks **directly above**, so one field covers
all three positions:

| `insert_after_id` | result |
|---|---|
| omitted | the new level becomes the LOWEST, below everything |
| any id | the new level sits immediately above that level |
| the highest level's id | the new level becomes the HIGHEST, above everything |

"After" reads against this list as a client displays it — lowest first — so the new level
appears immediately after the named one. Sending a raw `echelon_rank` instead would put the
dense numbering and the renumbering it needs in the caller's hands.

**400 if `insert_after_id` names a level that does not exist.** There is deliberately no
fallback to the top or the bottom: a client holding a stale list would otherwise renumber
every level in the system while the operator watched for a reason they could not see.

**409 if the name is already in use.** Names are unique across the vocabulary.

**THE NEW LEVEL IS NEVER A SYSTEM ROW**, so the CMS may offer to remove it. The four seeded
levels carry `is_system`, which stops the default hierarchy being deleted and leaving a
system whose vocabulary is a blank page.

response.name: The whole vocabulary after the insert, because the levels above moved.

item.name: What one hull really carries from the weapon catalogue

query.description:
The hull whose OWN allowances are being read or replaced.

**A SECOND DECLARATION OF THE SAME QUERY PARAMETER, because the OPTIONALITY differs and OpenAPI 3.0
states `required` on the parameter itself rather than at the point of use.** `ForUnit` above is the
same `for_unit` used as a FILTER on a catalogue list, where its absence is the ordinary "show me
everything"; these routes have no such reading, so theirs is required. One object cannot be both, and
the wire name is identical — both declare `name: for_unit`.

**REQUIRED ON THESE ROUTES, AND OPTIONAL ON THE CATALOGUE LIST.** The same parameter both places, with
the opposite optionality, because the role differs: on a catalogue list it NARROWS a collection the caller
could read anyway, so its absence is the ordinary "show me everything"; here it names the SUBJECT, so its
absence leaves the route with nothing to describe.

An id that is not a live hull is a **400 naming this field** — not an empty list, which would say
"this hull may be given nothing" about a hull that does not exist.

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/weapons`.

**THE FLEET'S OWN RECORD, NOT A PERMISSION.** `GET /weapons?for_unit=` answers what the hull MAY be
given, and `/weapons/allowances` answers what it declares for ITSELF; this answers what it HAS — a quantity
per catalogue entry, recorded by an operator and constrained by neither of the other two.

**EVERY ROW CARRIES `allowed`**, the maximum the register permits this hull today, resolved by the same
ladder the `for_unit` read uses. `null` means nothing permits it any more: it was never declared, or the
declaration was removed. That is the DISAGREEMENT this read exists to show — it is neither refused nor
silently corrected, because the register is what ships MAY be given and not a census of what they have.

**A RETIRED ENTRY IS NOT SHOWN AND ITS HOLDING IS NOT DESTROYED.** Retirement keeps what points at the
row, so a hull that really carried something before it was withdrawn keeps the record, out of sight — and
the write below cannot reach it either, which is what makes a screen's round trip lossless.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/weapons` — the same pair as `PATCH /weapons/{id}`, because both
write this catalogue's data rather than the hull register.

**IT REPLACES ONE HULL'S HOLDINGS AND NOTHING ELSE.** Another hull's record, and this hull's holdings in
the other two catalogues, are untouched: the delete is scoped to the hull in the query and to the kind in
the path.

**AN EMPTY ARRAY CLEARS THE HULL**, which is how a ship is discharged. A holding the body does not name is
dropped, which is what makes this a replace rather than a merge.

**AN ENTRY THE REGISTER DOES NOT PERMIT IS ACCEPTED.** Nothing is refused, reduced or clamped for
disagreeing with the allowance: the register is not a census, and the answer to a disagreeing record is to
SHOW it — the response carries `allowed` on every row, `null` where nothing permits it. The client chose
this over refusing the record and over clamping it (2026-10-12).

Refusals name the line: an entry that is not a live row of this catalogue is a **400 naming
`holdings[i].id_equipment`**, as is the same entry sent twice.

request.description:
Requires the `retire` action on `/system/weapons`. **No request body** — the verb says
everything, and the actor comes from the token.

**A TOMBSTONE, NOT A DELETE.** The row keeps its audit columns and its author, and stops
appearing in every list. `unit_equipment_allowances` still points at it, which is the point: the
record of what a hull MAY be given survives, and a hard delete would take it.

**It is not idempotent in its ANSWER.** A second call is `404`, because the row is no longer
live — the answer is about the row's state, and a client that retires twice has lost track of
it. `DELETE /weapons/{id}/image` is the idempotent one, because there the question is about a
picture rather than a row.

Because both unique indexes are partial on `deleted_at IS NULL`, retiring releases the name and
the code for reuse.

request.description:
Removes the picture. Requires the `update` action on `/system/weapons` — the same capability that
governs SETTING one, so "what may be changed about this weapon" stays a single question.

**THE OTHER HALF OF THE PAIR.** A picture is SET by the optional `file` part of `POST` and `PATCH`,
and an absent part there means "leave it alone" — a rule that has to exist, or renaming a weapon
would blank its photograph as a side effect. That rule is exactly what makes clearing inexpressible
as a missing part, so removal is a verb of its own. It is the same arrangement the hull path
reached in B29, from the other direction.

**It is idempotent, and the response does not say which case it was.** A row with no picture
returns `200` — a client retrying, or clearing from a list that went stale, asked for the
picture to be gone and it is gone.

**The row is cleared before the object is touched.** A failure between the two leaves
unreferenced bytes in the bucket, which cost storage and nothing else; the opposite order would
leave a row naming an object that is not there, and every read would presign that name into a
URL that 404s. The object delete is best-effort and logged rather than reported.

Nothing is returned. Re-read to confirm — `image_url` will be **absent**.
